Mr. Speaker, I would like some clarification. Am I finishing my magnificent speech on second reading, or can I now speak on the closure motion?
Some farmers need cash now to meet their payments to the Farm Credit Corporation, to clean up their fuel bills from their harvest and for a host of other things. There are many places in this country where at the moment their produce either cannot be sold or there is so much of it, it should not be sold. Why victimize agricultural producers for something that is no fault of theirs, that was not of their doing or their creation?
As I pointed out before and repeat, we provide interest free loans, which will never be paid, to the corporate sector through deferred corporation taxes, about $40 billion worth. That is an interest free deferment of taxes which are deferred forever. But the government wants to deny farmers interest free cash advances, which they have always repaid in full. This flies in the face of what used to be a very good-they did not have very many- policy of the Conservative Party. In fact, the political parties in the prairie provinces were united on this issue back in the 1940s and 1950s. The stubborn Liberal

I have yet to hear any good, sound reason from anybody in this House as to the necessity for doing this, or some reason for doing it, any kind of a reason. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak to this bill. I am very disappointed that this government has again taken this jackboot approach to closure. It is a terrible day for the farmers of this country. This government has invoked closure more times than we have had legislation before this House. It is time that the government went back to the farming community, consulted with them and used the legislation that is now in place to make available to them the moneys that they so desperately need at this time of the year.
The original advance payment program, which this bill now wants to change, was designed with the basic goal of establishing an orderly market system for Canadian farm products, one which ensured that supply met demand and that prices remained relatively stable. This program was meeting that goal satisfactorily.
Government Orders
Farmers require a substantial input at the beginning of the season, and so at harvest time they are eager to pay off the debts arising from this input. However, if they dump their entire crop onto the market at this time, several negative things happen. A flooded market means low prices for producers, an over-stressed processing and transportation system and a produce shortage would accompany high prices for consumers in the spring. That is the result of the financial pressure on producers to sell their entire crop at harvest time.
Since the advance payments program has been implemented, Canada has enjoyed an orderly marketing system which is the envy of many countries. The basic factor in this success has been the interest free loans advanced to producers through their producer organizations and guaranteed by the federal government at harvest time.
With Bill C-36, the government is eliminating the interest free component of the loan program. In doing so, it will cripple the already vulnerable family farm in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture has tried to soften the blow by telling farmers that by losing the interest free loans they will be doing their share to overcome Canada's deficit. Well, when the banks foreclose on their farms and their families lose their livelihood, I am sure that the farmers will rest easy knowing that they are helping to cut the government's deficit.
The issue of cost effectiveness has been explored by my colleagues on this side of the House, but I believe that its importance cannot be over-emphasized. Just how much will the government save by making the farmers pay interest on their loans through this program? The minister says that the amendments to this program will save the government approximately $20 million in this fiscal year. Dozens of farm organizations from Atlantic potato producers to Ontario com producers to western grain producers have told this government that without the interest free component of the program, the program will be too expensive for many producers. These same organizations have told the government again and again that the advantages of this program far outweigh the costs.
The government will find out too late that there is a cost in destroying the interest free program, a cost collected not only in dollars, but in a much more

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
intangible and valuable coin, that of the survival of the family farm.
Passage of this legislation would mean higher costs for farmers at a time when our family farm is under siege already, as we can see daily in the reports of farm foreclosures and bankruptcies.
Farming organizations in western Canada estimate that eliminating the interest free component of the program will increase borrowing costs in the range of $1,500 to $2,000 per year per farm. Skyrocketing interest rates resulting from the government's irresponsible fiscal policies will play their part in crushing farmers under growing debt. Government savings simply do not translate into farmer savings.
In other words, without the interest free aspect, the advance payments program will be rendered virtually useless to farmers.
The Ontario Com Producers Association which, in the past years, has seen approximately 2,000 producers participate in the program has stated that eliminating the interest free provision will result in an ineffectual program with minimal participation.
What is this government's tme motive in proposing this measure? It is true that if producers are discouraged from participating and the program dies from neglect then the government will save money. Is this the tme plan? The destruction of the interest free advance payment program is only a step in the federal government's increasingly obvious assault on the family farm in Canada.
Cutbacks in transportation subsidies, budgets for dairy export programs and support for organizations such as the Canadian Dairy Commission, to name but a few, have resulted in farmers losing $400 million in support structures since the last election. This is not even counting the damage that Bill C-36 promises to do.
Industries such as wine and tobacco are floundering. Marketing boards have been drastically weakened. The effects of the free trade agreement hold little promise for the farmers of this country.
While the government pays lip service to the preservation of the family farm in Canada, it cripples its future by
destroying these mechanisms which have allowed it to survive thus far in a cut-throat global market-place.
We have seen countless times this government's disregard for ordinary Canadians, its abdication from the unemployment insurance program, its gutting of our national rail system, its multi-pronged attack on Atlantic Canada and, most recently, in its proposed goods and services tax. That this government pays heed only to big business is painfully obvious. We need not be surprised but certainly angered by its attack on the family farm.
The interest free cash advance program has not only bolstered the Canadian marketing system to the benefit of producers, but to the benefit of millions of consumers as well. These ordinary consumers will also suffer from the destruction of this program.
With interest growing on their debts from harvest time onward, farmers will naturally be under great pressure to sell all of their produce and begin paying off their massive debts immediately, especially considering the high interest rates. The result will be low prices and spiraling debts for producers, a swamped quota system which, until now, has been the envy of the world and subsequent higher prices for consumers due to produce shortages next spring. This, in turn, necessitates higher imports from the U.S. which are often of an aged and inferior quality. This will be the result of a badly controlled market which this government's policy will create.
The government has tried to foist its guilt off on this side of the House belating that by our determination to save the existing advance payment program through debate we are only delaying urgently needed payments to farmers. If so, how does the government explain the dozens of producer organizations that have joined us in insisting that this bill is badly flawed? How does this government explain the fact that the Prince Edward Island Federation of Agriculture, the Ontario Com Producers Association, the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association and many other organizations have expressly requested that the government not implement this bill?
Such respected bodies such as the Advisory Committee to the Canadian Wheat Board unanimously resolved to recommend that the federal government operate the cash advance program as usual for the 1989-90 crop year
October 26, 1989

and only propose amendments after consultation with the producer organizations.
Of course, in the implementation of its agenda, the government has never shown much interest in seeking the input of those Canadians who will be most affected by the measures. From a finance committee that considered originally only going to two cities in Atlantic Canada and a Minister of Transport who refused to meet with municipal officials, this government obviously does not want to hear what Canadians have to say.
The Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues are turning a deaf ear to all of the producer organizations coast to coast that oppose this bill. This government's arrogance is stunning and will not be forgotten by farmers and other Canadians.
I find it appalling that the government will go forward at this time with this bill when farmers and producers so greatly need money at this time of year. They need their credit line and then be able to go to the banks when they have to borrow more money to keep their operations afloat.
This could not come at a worst time for Canadian farmers, when they are fighting all the effects and the impacts of the free trade agreement and the threat to their marketing policies. Again I would urge this government to go back to these organizations and negotiate a bill that will be much more beneficial. I ask it to keep this program intact, certainly for this year as has been recommended by all these producer organizations.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate.
I think the essence of what we are trying to do here is put in place the amendments to the Advance Payments for Crops Act and also the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.

The interest charges on that debt would curtail the activities of any government. I say that not in any partisan way because it would not matter which party was in charge here. The size of the national debt and the interest charges that have to be paid on it are, without a

doubt, a formidable obstacle and, in essence, shackle the abilities of government to be able to continue to deliver the programs we have now, let alone to improve upon them.
I think that producers across Canada understand the problem and the dilemma that faces the government. I think they understand also that the answer to the problem is not just to raise taxes, but that there also have to be some reductions in government spending.
In the recent budget, there were reductions. Every department of the government was asked to make some contribution to deal with the deficit problem. Of course, it is natural that each and every one of those proposals would be opposed by the opposition because that is their job, and by various groups affected in the country.
The fact is that most people across the country understand that these things have to be done. There is no great desire on the part of the government to inflict pain or hurt. The problem is that unless the deficit is addressed in some meaningful fashion at this time, we will soon reach the point where all of the revenue of government is taken up in interest charges, in servicing the debt of the past. Clearly, that cannot continue very long.
In regard to the amendments to these bills, the essence of them is this: That farmers will still be able-

Mr. Speaker, your point of course is well taken and I think illustrates the fact that I am sure the producers of this country would want members on all sides to get on with the business of Parliament to pass this legislation and to make the cash advances available to the farm community.
I wanted to take a couple of moments to outline a couple of the proposals that are in this bill. Of course, farmers will still be able to obtain financing to carry their crops from harvest time to delivery. They can still take advantage of marketing opportunities. The advances will be administered through producer organizations with which the federal government has agreements. The advance is extended to the farmer by the producer organization and is repaid by the farmer when the crop is delivered. The federal government will guarantee these advances against default so that the organizations and lenders involved take no risk.
What are the changes that are the subject of debate here? First, to provide better security, the act will guarantee payment of interest as well as the principal of the advance itself.
Second, under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, the interest rates will be designated by the minister rather than by regulation. This should assist in getting the advances into producers' hands more quickly.
Third, the advance limits would be designated by the minister up to a higher level than previously. Finally, interest rates will be based on rates negotiated by the Canadian Wheat Board or other producer organizations with the lending institutions. These rates will be significantly lower than would be the case if producers organizations sought credit independent of the federal guarantee.
In so far as orderly marketing is concerned, surely it is up to the producer to decide when to deliver within the schedules that are prescribed by the particular organization so that when the marketing agency-and I refer here to the Canadian Wheat Board as being of special interest to producers within my constituency-wants a particular grain or a crop delivered, they will open quota. It is of course up to the producer to decide to deliver. The fact that he is paying interest may indeed cause him to respond to the opening of quota and the request for delivery by the board. But that decision to ignore the request to the selling agency should be financed by the producer, not by the taxpayer. Of course, the price to the producer delivering is averaged throughout the year.
I want to spend some time on the background to this bill because I think it is being portrayed in some circles as some sort of heartless, vicious attack on the farm community. The fact is that nothing could be further from the truth. Unless serious steps are taken now to address the debt and deficit problem in this country, there simply will not be federal moneys available. Forget about interest free advances, there will not be any money available for fundamental farm programs, for the administration of the agriculture department, or indeed for the ordinary running of government departments, to say nothing about transfer payments to the provinces, or the support of our social safety net which we have come to appreciate and to enjoy. So there is a very fundamental issue at stake here.

I would like to make some reference to the magnitude of the debt at this point in time. The national debt and all of the accumulated deficits of the past amount to some $330 billion. We are told that that accumulated total of national debt will become $350 billion by spring. The interest payments that have to be made on that debt are in the neighbourhood of $35 billion to $39 billion a year. That is an enormous sum of money. It amounts to about $1,400 for every man, woman and child in this country. That amount has to be found to service the debt that was built up when the governments of the past failed to take in enough money, failed to tax Canadians sufficiently to pay for the programs that were delivered in the past.
That is the problem facing this government today, and, I might add, will have to be faced by whoever is in government. So again I stress that my remarks are intended to be as non-partisan as they can possibly be in this place. The figures do not change. The figures are there. The debt is there and it is inescapable. It will not go away. We cannot tear it up. We cannot renege on the treasury bills. We cannot renege on the Canada savings bonds. These are investments by Canadians in the main and they expect, of course, to receive interest on their investment.
We continue to try to find ways to deal with this problem. The size of the national debt has reached the point where the interest charges on it are feeding on themselves, like a snowball going down hill. Despite the best efforts of the past several years in terms of reducing government involvement, reducing the public service, in terms of eliminating non-essential programs, getting rid of a number of Crown corporations that were serving no useful public purpose, and in spite of some tax increases in the past, we still have this mounting debt.
It is clear that more has to be done. It is inescapable. It simply will not go away. We may be told that it is a heartless budget, and you cannot cut national defence, cut CBC, or reduce programs, but it has to be done some place. The only way that it is possible to deal with the debt and deficit problem is either to take in more money or to spend less.
There are two ways to take in more money. One is to increase taxes and another is to put more Canadians to work. Obviously government is moving in two thrusts.

Mr. Speaker, rural Canada is under siege. Services and institutions which have long been an integral part of the lives of rural Canadians are being dismantled and removed.
For generations the post office has been a focal point of our rural communities. Today Canada Post is slowly but relentlessly proceeding with its agenda to remove the post office from these communities. Mr. Speaker, the laundering of money from drug trafficking is a serious problem in Canada. Until last January when Bill C-61 was enacted, Canadian law never specifically made money laundering a crime. Bill C-61 encourages Canadian banks to establish their own private guidelines on what constitutes suspicious bank deposits.
I would like to commend the Royal Bank of Canada for going one step further by imposing a de facto reporting requirement for all large transactions. Since January, anyone making a large cash deposit at the Royal must sign a declaration of source of funds. That person must provide personal identification such as a social insurance number, passport or driver's licence. The signed form gives the bank permission to disclose the transaction to the police.
So far this year, the Royal has examined close to 100 suspicious accounts, and has reported 76 to the RCMR On October 12, 1989, U.S. criminal charges were laid against a Royal Bank customer after police were tipped off by the bank about suspicious transactions. Parliamentarians for Global Action have provided Canada with an opportunity to reverse its intransigence in the face of meaningful action in this area. Canada can and should join the over 39 countries that back the call for an amendment to the partial test ban treaty on nuclear weapons, an amendment that would turn the treaty into a comprehensive ban on nuclear tests.
If the world threat of nuclear weapons is to be overcome, progressive industrialized nations have to take up the challenge on behalf of humankind. Canada cannot let pass the occasion to show leadership, especially now that it has a seat on the Security Council.

Mr. Speaker, I am responding today to a report prepared by the PC Quebec caucus complaining that too much federal research and development money is spent in the National Capital Region. In complaining, the report ignores the fact that most departmental research is carried out in the National Capital Region as well as the concentration of federal laboratories operated by the National Research Council.
The report implied that the level of R and D spending in the National Capital Region is excessive and that more should be spent in Quebec. The Minister of Communications is quoted as saying that there is a problem and agreeing that his province should get more.
Although it is natural in politics, members of the House should avoid the temptation to jump on the bandwagon of demanding more R and D money for their regions. R and D is too important and the money is too scarce for it to be thrown into the political pork-barrel.
All regions in Canada should be doing more R and D, but you do not increase the level of R and D in Canada by moving existing activities from one region to another. Investment in science must take into account the best interest of science. Regional considerations should only play a role when international experts have made location one of the technical determinants. Politicians should not pretend to be experts when they are not.
I call upon all members of this House and upon the government to denounce the pernicious and parochial attitude about science revealed in the Tory caucus report.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear!

If these expressions of support will end, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday, the minister said that his 9 per cent GST on just about everything that moves could not be reduced. In Montreal last night, he refused to give Canadians assurance that it would not increase.
Can we assume from these remarkable statements that in fact the GST will rise if it is introduced at the same rate as the manufacturers' sales tax has increased since this government has been in office?

Mr. Speaker, I was going to wish the hon. member all the best in his current endeavours but he seemed to turn that one off with the preamble to his question so I will restrain myself.
I have commented on a number of occasions in this House, as the hon. member is aware, on the very important balance that is in the package of measures that
form the GST system and the difficulty of changing just one of those. It is not possible. If people want lower rates, they have to accept a reduction in things like the credit to the middle income reduction or the payment to small business. Those are very important elements. I have just commented very specifically on the difficulty of making changes to those very important fairness elements in the package.
The hon. member has commented on the fact that I cannot make any guarantees for future governments. I am sure he understands that that is not possible to do. In this House I have said that barring unforeseen circumstances, we do not anticipate that rate changing.
However, those are things that any government has to maintain some flexibility on.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance talks about balance in the system. One of the problems is that most ordinary Canadians see the system that he is advocating as being severely imbalanced in favour of the rich as compared to the poor.
I would simply direct this question to the minister. In view of the record of this government which in its time in office has increased the manufacturers' sales tax from 9 per cent to 10 per cent to 11 per cent to 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent, would it not be fair for the taxpayers to assume that if this tax is introduced, on the basis of the government's record that eventually the taxpayers are going to be bled dry by increases in the GST just as they were by the manufacturers' sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member has raised two points that I would like to address. The first is that he says that this new GST system is weighted against those with lower incomes and favours those with upper incomes.
Let me remind the hon. member that when we came into office low income people were paying two or three percentage points more of their income in sales tax than people in upper income brackets. But, with the refundable sales tax credit and now the goods and services tax credit under the proposed system, those with low incomes will pay two percentage points less of their income in sales tax than those in upper incomes. Clearly we have shifted the whole balance of the sales tax system in favour of those in lower income brackets.
October 26, 1989

The hon. member has raised a second point relating to what could happen in the future. The only assurance that any taxpayer has that tax rates will not increase is if a government controls its spending. We have controlled program spending of the Government of Canada to 3.5 per cent over the last five years, on average. That is less than the rate of inflation.
In that same period of time the average of the provinces has been 6.4 per cent. One province, Ontario, has raised its program spending, on average, 9.5 per cent. That is the best assurance. If we continue that record of keeping program spending lower than the provinces, that is how Canadians can be assured that the tax burden will not be increased.

Mr. Speaker, the average taxpayer is going to be interested in that carefully crafted answer which ignores the additional $2,000 a year in tax being paid by ordinary taxpayers.
The minister asks us to trust him. The Auditor General pointed out in his report that 1,500 tax collectors could not collect the manufacturers' sales tax from
75,000	accounts, with either adequacy or fairness, and that that has been a cost to the ordinary taxpayer.
How does the minister think it is possible that one million accounts are going to be served by only a two to threefold increase in the number of collectors without adding still a greater burden on the shoulders of the ordinary taxpayer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me draw to the attention of the hon. member the difference between the existing federal sales tax and the goods and services tax. Under the existing tax for those 75,000 taxpayers there are 22,000 separate deals between Revenue Canada and the individual taxpayers. These have developed over the years.'They have resulted in the most complex form of sales tax system that anyone can imagine anywhere.
Surely the hon. member can understand why we want to move away from that system into a far more simple system, the goods and services tax, which will require far fewer people per taxpayer to administer and will allow us to ensure that there is not the same sort of tax avoidance that is there under the existing system, to which the Auditor General has referred. That, we have said, is one
Oral Questions
of the key reasons we must move from the existing system to a new system where there will not be that same form of tax avoidance.

The all-party Standing Committee on the Environment spent the last two days in Washington, D.C. encouraging Congress to do the right thing: to hold firm on cutting S02 emissions by at least 10 million tonnes by the year 2000 and to cap new emissions.
Canada has yet to legislate a national cap on acid rain. Will the minister assure this House that there will be a national legislated cap in place within the time frame we are urging on the United States, which will likely be Earth Day in April 1990?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, current control actions in the seven eastern most provinces of Canada have already resulted in a 40 per cent reduction in emissions. It is clear to this government that we cannot allow emissions to increase after that, so we need a cap.

This is an item on the agenda of the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment. We have a committee which is responsible for devising recommendations. We think the motto should be to secure a national cap in those seven provinces through negotiations at the CCME level and then to secure the cap through legislation. A possible motto could be, for example, what we did for the controls which presently exist, that is, to use the provincial legislation process.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-36, an act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Schneider (p. 5069).

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to stand today and speak on this very important piece of legislation which affects the advance payments to farmers in the riding of Essex-Kent as well as the farmers across Canada.
Bill C-36 intends to cancel the interest free provisions of the advance payments for crops and the prairie grain advance programs. The intention of this legislation is not acceptable to the Canadian farmer.
The government introduced this bill on September 27, 1989. At that time harvest across Canada was well under way. In my riding much of the harvest is complete. Yet we are debating legislation that has kept money out of the pockets of farmers in this country.
It is unfortunate that the legislation was introduced when it was when we stop and think that the farmers early in the spring had done a great deal of planning for their production. Very quickly, the government has changed the rules in the middle of the season. When farmers commenced their current year production they
Government Orders
arranged their financing on the basis of the advance payments they were expecting.
However, this government has chosen to change course in the middle of that. Today, the government has forced closure on this bill, not allowing the opposition, not allowing the government, not allowing the farm community within the country to be heard fairly and justly. Many people on this side of the House have stated how bad it is that the government would come forward with closure as many times as it has.
I, too, am a new member of this House and I am very concerned that every time a piece of legislation comes forward we are not allowed to speak clearly, fairly and openly on it. We are forced to closure. We are forced to sit long hours hoping that we will have an opportunity to speak, not necessarily given that opportunity on a regular basis.
Two days ago we debated Bill C-20, a taxation bill which the government claims is necessary as a transition to tax reform. Why does the government emphasize the need for transition legislation one day but not the next? Where is the transition for farmers on advance payments? There is none. The government refuses to provide interest free advance payments for crops and has suspended the past practice without any legislation in place.
The government would have Canadians and our farmers believe that it is the fault of opposition parties for not having the new bill in place. The proposed legislation is bad, and we must tell the government that it is bad. We are attempting to do that at this point in time.
We on the opposition side of the House are not alone in our criticism. Prairie Pools Corporation opposes the bill. That organization has formally requested the government to withdraw the bill at this time. It has indicated that a thorough review of the legislation is necessary to assess the impacts on cash flow and agricultural marketing. The corporation further noted that the existing Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act has proven valuable for providing the needed cash flow to producers and encouraged orderly marketing and efficient grain handling.
The National Farmers Union opposes the bill. This organization has also condemned the proposed legislation, requesting the government withdraw Bill C-36 and reinstate the current interest free legislation. It has

Government Orders
criticized Bill C-36 as being regressive. We on this side of the House agree with that assessment.
The existing prairie grain advance payment program enabled producers to save on interest costs. It allowed producers to meet debt obligations, assisted creditors to have accounts paid on time to settle outstanding accounts, relieved pressure on the Canadian Wheat Board elevators and the quota system from becoming clogged and assisted the board in programming orderly marketing and sales.
The National Farmers Union views these positive features as an integral part of the farming industry. The removal of the benefits, if Bill C-36 is passed, will be devastating to the farm community.
The Ontario Com Producers Association has also requested the Minister of Agriculture to abandon Bill C-36 and that the current programs be continued. The association is opposed to the elimination of interest free provisions of the current legislation because the relative cost of APCA marketing programs has been minimal compared to the benefits generated in the agricultural sector.
The program has proven to be of major benefit in shifting corn sales from autumn until later in the marketing year, thereby reducing the extent of export sales in autumn and shortages induced by imports during later months. The net result has been financial benefits to producers, domestic users and commercial elevators.
The APCA program is not trade distorting. It does not stimulate production but rather encourages orderly marketing. The GATT Geneva Accord of early April obliges Canada to freeze existing support programs, not reduce them.
There is no offsetting reduction for the 1989-90 crop year in the U.S. loan program-the American equivalent for the APCA-for grains and oilseeds. Canadian grain and oilseed producers are already contributing their share to the national debt via the programs in excise sales tax, sales tax exemptions on diesel fuel and on gasoline.
All of these farming organizations are prepared to meet with the Minister of Agriculture to review proposals on advance payments. That point must be clearly
understood. The organizations are willing to have open discussions. We encourage this. But what they are saying is do not arbitrarily change the rules of the game half way through a season. The crops are not only planted for the most part they are harvested as well. Farmers depend upon these advance payment incentives.
According to this government's budget in the next two years farmers will see reductions such as crop insurance by $200 million; grain and flour transportation by $40 million; branch line rehabilitation by $32 million; grain and crops advance payments by $54 million; dairy export by $14 million; commodity based loans by $14.5 million; dairy commission by $14 million; and excise tax and fuel rebates by $100 million.
How much are we going to ask the farm community to sacrifice? Are we going to tax the withdrawal programs until the Canadian farmer cannot afford to be in business? Farmers are asking, "Where will it end?".
Other farming organizations, including the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board, B.C. Vegetable Marketing Commission, and the Saskatchewan Canola Growers Association, to name a few, have echoed their colleagues' concerns and requests to reinstate the current programs of advance payments.
Farmers, farming organizations, marketing boards, elevator operators, farm financiers-literally thousands upon thousands of Canadians-believe in the benefits of the advance payments program. Everyone involved in agriculture believes in these programs. The only people not in favour are the members opposite. Does that say something about the government? I think it does.
Farmers in my riding are upset. They are upset that this government does not care about them anymore. Farmers are being asked to make concession after concession on their incomes, concessions that will cost the farming community $400 million in the next two years. These restrictions must cease. These loss of dollars to the farm community cannot be carried through week after week, month after month. We must reverse these ill-conceived actions of the government. Farmers deserve better. Let us begin now to show them that we do care.
I implore the government to reverse these anti-farming initiatives and let the farming community survive.
October 26, 1989

This morning hon. colleagues on the other side of the House brought forth the fact that we are several billion dollars in debt. We have been hearing that echoed in the House time after time. The members of the government have continually stated that it was the fault of a previous Liberal government. Canadian people are not that naive. After five years in power, the government has increased the debt $150 billion, doubled the national debt, and at the same time continually blamed their predecessors for the problems.
It is time to face reality. It is time to stop blaming somebody who was in government five years ago. It is time to carry through initiatives that are required. It seems to me the government is heading in a very wrong direction. It is going after the farm community, the weaker people in our society, and that will devastate this country.
It is time this government changed its direction and came to the reality that Canadian people are important, not just the farm community, but all of those who are weaker in our society. I believe the government has overlooked this important fact.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising in the House today to address this government's intention to withdraw the interest free provision for prairie grain advance payments and advance payments for crops.
At first glance, Canadians might wonder what all the fuss is about. After all, we are only talking about some $25 million to $27 million which farmers could surely sacrifice seeing how this government feels so strapped for cash, could they not?
I am glad I have this opportunity to speak in the House on the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act changes because it is through measures such as this that we can see how this government is mistreating Canada's farmers.
This piece of legislation raises so many issues that illustrate what this government is all about. It raises the issues of confusion, incompetence, and I might add, spinelessness. While I am glad I have been given the opportunity to defend Canadian farmers' interests, I am sorry the government would even put forth such a piece
Government Orders
of legislation in the first place, that we should have a debate on whether we provide farmers with a program that works, or do we take it away and slap Canadian farmers in the face?
Unfortunately, this government's agenda seems to require dismantling good programs. At the rate it is going, by the end of its term it will have done more damage to the effective institutions in this country than any other government in Canadian history, that is, unless it begins to listen to what Canadians are saying, to come up with creative and positive reforms, and to abandon their cut and slash attitude.
The changes to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, which are being proposed, provide one example of what I mean by the mindless cut and slash policy of this government. At stake is approximately $27 million for Canadian farmers, farmers who store their grain in the fall and collect an advance payment for it which they will sell in the spring or early summer when grain prices are higher and the fall grain glut is cleared.
The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds claims he is not trying to prevent farmers from using this program. He is simply going to charge them interest on partial payment for grain stored six to eight months over the winter.
I have news for the minister. When the government eliminates the interest free provision in this act, it discourages farmers from using the program. In effect, the government is discouraging the storage of grain, impacting negatively on the elevator storage industry, on Canada's food security, as well as on Canadian farmers. Without the interest free provisions of the advance payment program, and with the increased administrative costs to the farmer under this legislation, the attractiveness of this program to the average farmer is lost. Then one day, who knows, this government might come along and tell farmers they are not using this program very much and cut it completely. It would not surprise me one bit, seeing as the effectiveness of the program would have been cut with Bill C-36.
What might happen with the prairie grain advance payments program, may be the same tactic the Minister of Transport is using with VIA Rail, wound and then move in for the kill; cut the effectiveness of the service now, and when it is down on its knees, stamp it out for good. One less bother for the government.

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
I would like to expand on why the program should continue to exist as it does now, because it seems to me that the government does not think these things out for itself. What is worse is the fact that when the opposition points out the flaws in the government's reasoning, the government gets too embarrassed to make the proper changes. Instead, it blames the entire mess on the opposition. It is the only way that the members opposite think they can save face after having bungled this legislation. By failing to listen to the reasons this opposition and 19 producer groups across Canada have been trying to communicate to the government, I am afraid they are only making matters worse.
Let us first look at what is at stake for the government. Cutting the interest free provisions for advance payments would mean roughly $25 to $27 million for the government treasury. While this $25 million makes this program beneficial and worth while for farmers, it is a drop in the bucket for the government when compared to the revenue generated from taxes on products generated on farms, almost $1 billion on alcohol beverages and $1.8 billion on tobacco, just to name two.
As my colleague from Lambton-Middlesex pointed out, the government collects about $3.5 billion in excise and sales taxes on tobacco and alcohol products. Yet, it complains that it cannot afford $25 million for a program that has been working very well in favour of orderly marketing in Canada for the last 30 years.
I wonder why this particular $25 million is so crucial all of a sudden, and why this government would rather face the wrath of Canadian farmers than put its own house in order. What can one expect from a confused government that digs itself into a bigger and bigger hole by raising interest rates, increasing its deficit, increasing taxes, all the while dragging the Canadian economy into the hole with it.
Maybe we are seeing a continuation of this government's policy of breaking down Canada's orderly marketing system in favour of free market enterprise to comply with secret agreements made in the free trade negotiations, just like in the softwood lumber dispute, when we gave up our bargaining chips before we got to the table.
As my hon. colleagues across the floor must know, this program does not even lead to trade distortions. It simply
encourages the orderly marketing of our grains, com, and other crops. I am afraid that I fail to see this government's justification for chipping away at the financial management tools that have been so valuable to the farmers in the past.
We on this side of the House understand the need to control the deficit. What we disagree with is the government's affinity for making cuts that affect the poor, the sick, the elderly, the unemployed, as well as small businessmen and farmers, while paving the road, I might add, for big business, multinational corporations and the wealthy. Members opposite should know that the mark of a country's government is how it treats its weakest members, not its strongest.
I would like to end by making a plea, as all members on this side have done, to the members opposite, to vote against this legislation because of its severe implications for orderly marketing in Canada. A vote against Bill C-36, is a vote for common sense, for Canadian farmers, and for the institutions that have allowed our agriculture community, indeed, all of us to prosper.

Mr. Speaker, we are facing a closure motion which I think was totally unnecessary and uncalled for in this particular instance. We have been debating Bill C-36, which is an act to take away the interest free cash advances that farmers in western Canada have had since 1957. The reasons the government is giving for that are totally bogus.
We listened to the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia tell us that the government is faced with a huge debt. That is something we all know. He attempted to blame it on the NDP. Apparently it was all our fault because we defeated the government of Joe Clark. We do feel some responsibility for that. I think we were very much vindicated in 1984 when we saw not Joe Clark but a different leader lead the Conservative Party to form a government.
Under that leadership the accumulative deficit and debt of this country more than doubled in the first four years. It took Liberals some 120 years to accumulate a bit over $150 billion, and according to the words of the member for Swift Current, we have now passed $320 billion, which is more than twice that debt, and heading
October 26, 1989

for $350 billion or $360 billion by spring when this fiscal year is finished.
So it was a good thing we defeated the Conservatives in 1979, or we would have had that kind of deficit as well as the last five years with which to deal. We would have been dealing with far more debt than we are now.
The member attempted to show that the taking away of a $27 million expenditure for interest free cash advances would somehow cure this huge debt that his government has placed on the shoulders of the Canadian people. Somehow $27 million is going to rectify that. How ludicrous. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that $27 million will not even pay the interest on that debt for six hours? The minor debate that has occurred on this bill has gone just over six hours, and the interest has been ticking away on the national debt accumulated by this Conservative government and the more than the $27 million that it is proposing to save with this proposal has already been spent, just as that few hours ticked away. It is a ludicrous kind of argument, but it gets even more stupid when one looks at the true economics of it.
With the availability of the interest free cash advances, farm producers right across the country have made good use of their ability to hold product from the market in order that the market not be flooded with product. Fruit and vegetable producers have used it to good advantage. The cash advance system has permitted them to keep the product in storage, so that the price rises. That is important, not only to farm incomes, but also to government deficits and government expenditures.
With the kind of "force the product on to the market" approach that the current government is taking with this particular proposal, it will be forced by other measures that this country adopted years ago to pay agricultural stabilization payments because when this action forces the price of farm produce down, other government funds are expended to bring farm incomes up.
I will demonstrate how important this is. Not only does it have that effect, but it reduces government income. With the advantage of higher prices, which farmers are able to take advantage of now that they are sprinkling their produce on to market when demand is there, farmers occasionally have to pay income tax, because their incomes are higher. With this stupid and short-
Govemment Orders
sighted action, the government is forgoing the collection of far more than the $27 million worth of income tax.
I said that I would give you some examples of how this works, Mr. Speaker. Let us look at figures from the Ontario Corn Producers Association which point out, according to their calculations, that in the crop year of 1986-87, the fact that interest free cash advances were available resulted in the average price of corn going up $4.54 per tonne. They report that this meant that over-all all of the producers benefited by approximately $2,044,800 as a result. What did it cost the government for the farmers to make that kind of saving from the market? That year it cost Agriculture Canada $1,175,000, so they got pretty close to two for one return on their investment.
The following year was even better. In the 1987-88 crop year, instead of dumping their product at the beginning of the crop period, the benefit to the producer from being able to market his product in an orderly fashion and sprinkling it on to the market for a 12-month period, resulted in the producers gaining a little better than $36 a tonne for a final price. That meant that all of the com producers in Ontario benefited by $16.8 million at a cost to the federal treasury of a mere $1.1 million, which was the cost of maintaining the interest free cash advance. There was a better than sixteen for one return on the government's expenditure. You can be very certain, Mr. Speaker, that on that extra $16 million that Ontario com producers received, a lot of income tax was paid and the government probably had returned many times over the small expenditure laid out for the interest free cash advances.
I have some similar figures here from soybean producers in Ontario, who report that in the crop year 1987-88, they estimate that there was an advantage to them of being able to utilize the cash advance system in that year of just over $60 per tonne, a total of $10.7 million for that crop year. It cost the federal government $773,000. That is a very good return for the Government of Canada for its small investment. The returns in income tax payments alone would have far exceeded the expenditures they made. The market stayed up to the point where stabilization payments coming out of another government envelope were not necessary.

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
It is a foolish set of economic arguments that the government is trying to foist on the farm community. Farmers are much too clever to buy that argument. There are some who are not so clever, and it is very unfortunate. I and perhaps some other members have received a letter from the Premier of Saskatchewan who is also the Minister of Agriculture for that province. He is writing, he says, "to express our concern", and I think it is the royal "our", "at the delay which Saskatchewan farmers are currently experiencing in being able to apply for cash advances on their crops, and to encourage you, as your party's agriculture critic, to work towards a speedy resolution to this problem. This delay is causing considerable hardship for many of this province's producers, who rely on the cash advance program to meet a number of their financial obligations."
Then he goes on and tells a mistruth. He says:
As you know, cash advances cannot be issued until such time as Bill
C-36, an act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, is passed by Parliament.
Such rubbish! The Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act have been in effect in this country for years and years. There is nothing stopping the government from putting that program into effect, except their own stubbornness and stupidity. All they have to do is give the directive. Parliament has spoken. We have presented them with the law. We have presented them with the power to do it. Why don't they do it?
Did Premier Grant Devine, in his divine wisdom, write to the Minister of Agriculture and ask him to please obey the law and make cash advances available? He does not seem to have. Did he write to the Prime Minister and tell him how concerned he was about forcing the farmers he speaks for to pay even more interest? You would think that he would have, but it does not seem that he did. That is strange, because this is the man who convinced the premiers at a premiers' conference last summer that they should be putting pressure on the federal government to do something about interest rates. Here was his great opportunity to ask the government, as politely as he could, to please obey the law and provide these funds at zero rate of interest to the farm community. Did the Premier of Saskatchewan say anything about that? No, he does not seem to have bothered to write them. He wrote me, a member of the third party in opposition,
asking me to quickly change the law so his producers could start paying more interest on an already very difficult burden of debt that those producers are paying now.
As the Premier of Saskatchewan and having divine wisdom, he should know all about the problems of carrying debt. He seemed to understand it a year ago when he carried the message on behalf of the premiers about high interest rates. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, he came to Ottawa, gave the message, was so persuasive that as he was climbing the steps of the plane, the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada announced that interest rates had just gone up a half of 1 per cent.
This premier and this Minister of Agriculture is also the person that knows the effects of interest rates on his own fanners, because he is the man who got himself re-elected in 1986 on a program of low interest and no interest loans to his farmers. Then as soon as he was elected, he made those loans collect a rather high rate of interest, 50 per cent higher than he had indicated it would be during the election campaign.
Not only that but he is out there collecting those loans. He has declared a great many of them bad loans, and he has put collection agencies on over 4,500 farmers in the province of Saskatchewan. That is how concerned he is about the rise in interest rates. He is concerned because he has got himself in the position of being just like one of the banking institutions and just like this federal government that see things from the point of view of the banks, and the international grain companies, but do not see things from the point of view of the people they were elected to represent.
There are a couple of other things that the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia used as excuses for introducing this legislation. He tried to convince the House that with the added burden of paying interest on cash advances that farmers would be forced to deliver their grain earlier. Of course, it may have that effect. It certainly will in the open market crops. The Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec have told us that they see producers of turnips and some of the fruit and vegetable crops being forced to market their produce in about six or eight months instead of over a full 12-month period. That would have the effect of putting pressure on agricultural prices at the beginning of the year, and end up with consumers having to rely on
October 26, 1989

imported produce which is going to be much more expensive for the last part of the year.
This does nothing for producers or consumers, but it is helpful to the banking business, because when the banks lend money to the Wheat Board or some of the farm groups under this interest free program the rate is much lower because it is a government rate. Now, the credit rating will be slightly different and the costs will be up a wee bit, and they will receive a fraction or a full percentage point, perhaps in some of the smaller groups as much as 2 percentage points more, and their take will be increased. The international grain cartels will love it. The purchasers of fruits and vegetables will love it because it will force prices down at the beginning of the year. Consumers seldom get that price reflected in the stores. It provides an opportunity for greater profits for those handlers, but it means disaster for farmers.
It will have a tendency to push down net farm incomes. As I pointed out earlier in my speech, there will be some commodities where the downward effect will be so strong that in fact it will trigger payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Act and the government will be paying out money in spite of itself. For the simple maintenance of this program, at a cost of some five or six hours of interest that the government is paying anyway, it would be able to leave the farm community and the rural community in a position where their prices would be going up to the point where income tax revenues would be collected instead of subsidy payments going out to the farm community. That, in our mind, is good business.
This party of Conservatives is doing this because it does not agree with orderly marketing, cannot understand the value of that to the farming community, and have decided it has to kowtow to the banks and international grain cartel and some of the Americans who are saying that we have to do away with the Wheat Board and marketing boards. It has decided to kowtow to that, make a nod in that direction, and begin the process of undermining prices and the ability of farmers to get their cost of production out of the market.
In conclusion, I think that this legislation demonstrates that this government is once again refusing to be effective and efficient in its management of the economy and, in particular, in its management of affairs that affect rural Canada. In its presenting the closure motion, it has demonstrated an equal disregard for communication and for reality. Had it proceeded at a regular pace, I am sure
Government Orders
the bill would have been through by now. When it starts using closure, members are inclined to make a speech to complain about that. Had the government used common sense, this could have been before the committee where the farm organizations and the farm groups need to be heard, because the government has obviously decided it is not going to listen to us or believe us. The farm groups have to be heard. They know how this will affect them. I think we have to hear every farm group in those communities.

Mr. Speaker, once again members of Parliament have the opportunity to speak on this very important issue. Once again, we will endeavour to try to make this minister and the government understand how important the interest free provision is to Canadian farmers.
This program was put in place to encourage orderly marketing of product. It has been very successful in achieving this goal by shifting sales from the fall when the crops are harvested to later on in the marketing year. This allows farmers the leeway to either play the market, or have the ability to market their product at a time when it is more reasonable and more equitable to do so. This program was put in place to encourage the orderly marketing of produce.
Historically, crop prices are the lowest on average at harvest time. The depressed prices are usually as a direct consequence of the eagerness of farmers to sell their crops soon after they are removed from the field. This eagerness is precipitated by two main factors: first, the need to generate cash to pay shopping expenses, the year end tax bills, and related financial operations; and uncertainties as to whether subsequent price increases will be sufficient to cover interest and storage carrying costs.
The advanced payment program under the Advance Payments for Crops Act has been one of the most effective means of countering historic marketing patterns and encouraging a more orderly marketing, that is, a greater percentage of crops are sold during the late winter, spring and summer rather than in the fall when all the congestion is in the market-place. Producers in the program have indeed benefited most of all, especially tobacco farmers in my riding. Even non-participants have benefited to some extent by experiencing relatively higher harvest time prices because of the reduced sale of the crop at this time of season. In other words, the market has not been flooded as it used to be before this

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
program came into effect, which resulted in depressed prices.
Those involved in commercial grain storage also benefit from holding over crops until market prices improve. Since the advance payments program was initiated in 1983-84 we have seen a substantial change in the marketing patterns. This has been a progressive step forward. To start fooling with this success is foolhardy, unreasonable and unfeeling, to say the least.
By making this change the government estimates it will save $27 million a year, hardly a large sum and hardly worth destroying a working and valuable program for. The minister and this government refuse to even try to understand how this measure will negatively affect Canadian farmers. They regularly ignore our advice and suggestions. You would think they would listen to the producers, the farmers themselves, who are most adversely affected by this program but they refuse to listen.
The government continues to bring in programs such as this which adversely affect a number of sectors of our economy and a number of Canadians without properly informing Canadians. There is no consultation and I call upon the government to move more toward a consultative process. It helps in the whole process of parliamentary democracy.
I never cease to be amazed by this government's approach. Time and time again it tried to rush bills through Parliament without consultation or thinking about the ramifications of these changes.
Closure all the time.

Closure all the time. I think there has been more closure within my first year here in Parliament than we have ever seen. That is not acceptable to people on this side of the House.
Although only 582 Canadian com farmers participated in the 1988-89 advance payments program, this low number was clearly a result of the small drought-reduced corn harvest this year. Many farmers throughout Ontario and indeed throughout Canada had a hard time last year during that period because of the drought program. Therefore, it is not surprising that the number
who actually participated in the program was low. In the three previous years when the crop size was more typical,
1,000	to 1,200 farmers participated. The number of tonnes involved was in the range of 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes or about 10 per cent to 15 per cent of the total marketed commercial Ontario corn crop. The government indicated that it could not agree with the suggestion of the Ontario corn producers that a participation rate of 10 per cent to 20 per cent means a relatively low benefit to the entire industry.
In the case of com, the 10 per cent to 15 per cent of the commercial crop involved in the program means that this quality of com is not sold into a glutted harvest-time market and is available for market needs later during the crop year. The benefit of this action extends to all producers and purchasers. In reality this is a benefit of the way that we have produced orderly marketing here in Canada. This is not the only orderly marketing area under attack by this government. We have seen that in the orderly marketing of our milk products and in many other orderly marketing areas of trade the government does not seem to be as committed as it says.
Let us look at the free trade deal. The government gave a commitment during the last election that under free trade the supply management or the orderly marketing of milk products would be protected. We have seen, as I and my colleagues have said time and time again, that there is no protection under the free trade agreement for orderly marketing of products. This is one more way to throw our marketing of agricultural products into a crisis. There is no way that Canadian farmers can orderly market not only grains but milk products under the free trade deal that we have in place now. Quite frankly, the Americans have not received the message. Americans have not acknowledged that we have orderly access into their market. What they have said is: "Yes, we signed the deal, but we fooled you. There is no way that we are going to allow your products into our market".
That throws into whack the whole question of marketing products in Canada. The recent GATT decisions have the same effect. GATT and other countries, led by the Americans, are attacking our supply of managed systems under Article II of GATT.
October 26, 1989

During the free trade debate the government said it would not be negotiated at GATT. We have seen that in fact it is. It said it would protect producers under the import control list. We found how effective that has been for our milk products for ice cream and yogurt. It has had absolutely no effect. In fact, the Americans are again attacking our marketing. This is just one more example of how our marketing systems are being attacked and being unduly represented by this government.
The Ontario corn producers also argue that it would be a flaw if most producers in most of the crops were enrolled in the program since this could mean a shortage of available crop at harvest time. Fortunately, with the program structured as it is at present, this has not occurred.
They also point out in their letter that while it is possible for organizations such as OCPA to borrow money using the APCA guarantee at about the prime rate of interest, the administration costs are significant, and it is not unreasonable to expect the full cost to the producer of prime plus 1 per cent or 2 per cent, depending on the amount of money borrowed. Administration costs include legal costs, inspection costs, lien registrations and office operations with the program.
In other words, it is going to be of no benefit to Canadian farmers. They are not going to get any advantage by going into this program. They have come to us and told us that. They want the people on this side of the House to stand up and let the government know that this program is no good. By not having the interest-free provision of the program, the government is in essence destroying it. It is making it totally useless for Canadian farmers.
The Ontario Corn Producers Association were particularly concerned with the suggestion that the presence of advanced payments represent an impediment to orderly marketing. Unfortunately, the implicit conclusion is that somehow the amendments inherent in Bill C-36 will reduce the incentive for storage which exists in the present program by encouraging sales, rather than storage. They strongly disagree that the advance payment programs have been disruptive to orderly marketing by discouraging timely sales.
Government Orders
They were also very disturbed that a desirability to encourage farmers to sell crops more quickly may be a reason for the amendments contained in Bill C-36. Like us, they strongly objected and disagreed with the suggestion that by opposing Bill C-36, farm organizations are depriving farmers of advanced payments for the 1989 crop.
In reality the present act authorizes such payments. OCPA filed an application for a 1989 program several months ago. Only reluctance by this minister to exercise authority spelled out in the existing legislation prevents funds from now being dispersed to crop producers across the country.
It was clearly lack of initiative by this minister to continue that program which is stopping funds from going to farmers now. Their final criticism is that Bill C-36 represents a reduction in federal support for Canadian farmers when no commitment has been made to reduce comparable assistance elsewhere, particularly in the United States. There is no such reduction in the U.S. farm bill loan provisions available to American farmers.
These are the arguments we have been putting forward to the government for many days now. Surely all farmers cannot be wrong. Before this government and this minister again reject the suggestion we have made to withdraw the bill and have some meaningful consultation with the producers who use this program, I have been asked by the farmers in Haldimand-Norfolk to ask this government to withdraw the bill, to sit down with farmers, have some meaningful consultation and get on with the program, instead of trying to bring in programs which are detrimental to their livelihoods.
Before making a rash decision to ram this bill through the House with its majority, I would suggest that it review the Auditor General's report which repeatedly takes the Department of Agriculture to task for the erosion of accountability and of parliamentary control. Just once maybe the government could be open-minded and realize that the farm organizations and members of Parliament are offering constructive suggestions to ensure that this program will continue to be a success.
As I mentioned in my previous speech, the minister has indicated that he wants to work closely with the provinces, farm organizations and others to plan and implement an improved policy network. Let us put action where his words are. Why does the minister not

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
prove to farmers that he cares about them, that he will consult with them and that he will put their ideas into legislation, not after the fact like this government has tended to do, but before it pushes through legislation without consultation.
I call on the minister to listen to their suggestions and concerns. They are defending their livelihoods. They are not sitting back and trying to bring in programs dealing with anybody else's livelihood, they are defending then-own livelihood. These people are good farmers and they deserve more than a bill that attacks their livelihood.
I urge the minister to stand up for farmers, stand up for agriculture, and withdraw this bill. I believe this bill will have a detrimental effect on farming.
I am concerned the way this minister has suggested that we on this side are delaying the bill somehow and that we are not giving farmers their livelihood.
They have many more members than us and if they wanted to bring in this bill they could have done so last week. Yet he goes across the country saying that we are the ones who are stopping their livelihood. Well, quite frankly, farmers in Canada are not fooled by that argument.
We have a case here today where the government brings in closure. This is the government's way of saying that we are delaying the bill. How many hours have we debated this major piece of legislation? We have spent four or five hours on a major piece of legislation that has wide-ranging effects on the farming communities of Canada. Surely we can debate this bill much longer than that.
I will close by saying that we, the farmers of Haldi-mand-Norfolk, reject this bill. They are not fooled by the government's argument that this bill will be anything but detrimental. On their behalf I call on this government to withdraw this bill. Do the honourable thing and withdraw the bill, consult with the farmers and try to bring in a more reasonable and fair approach to this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to
stand here today to speak on this bill that we are attempting to get through.
We had to bring in closure. I think all members of this House realize that we had to do that because of the delaying tactics of the Liberals and NDP who say that they are so much in favour of supporting farmers.
There have been discussions between our House leader and the House leaders of the two other parties with regard to these amendments. Since this House came back in September we have been trying to get an agreement in the House of Commons. The member who spoke previously is probably a new member and does not understand all of the nuances that go on in this House, but one of them is the attempt at co-operation of opposition parties, whether they be Liberal or NDP.
We have been trying to get this through since we came back to the House of Commons. We have had nothing but roadblocks from these people who are delaying it. Then they complain because we bring in closure. We bring in closure because the farmers in my community, the farmers in western Canada, the farmers right across this fair country of ours are waiting for this bill to go through so that those who want it can access the advance payments, those who want to do it.
Apply the law.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Well, well, well. My honourable friend from the NDP says: ''apply the law". Let me read to him some of the information. There is nothing in either the Advance Payments for Crops Act or the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act which requires guarantees of advance or advances to be made.
Nothing is stopping you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: If he would take the time to read it and understand what he is talking about when he stands in the House, he would know that section 4 of the Advance Payments for Crops Act provides that the minister may guarantee advances made by a producer organization.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Section 3 of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act states that the board may make advances on the initial payment for threshed grain to a producer. The word "may" in legislation does not compel an action to be taken. By not taking any action, the government is

therefore not acting contrary to the law and the hon. member knows that very well.
There is nothing stopping you from putting it in place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: All he wants to do is yell and not listen to what people are saying in this house. Open your ears and read my lips. I will send this over to the hon. member and he can read it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member listens with his mouth.
The law is there. Use it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Parliament passed a law that states he may. We are trying in this Parliament to amend the acts in such a way that it will allow a producer to receive not $30,000 in advance payments, not $60,000 in advance payment if there are two of them, not even $90,000. We are amending this law to allow a producer to receive $250,000 in advances.
How many will use that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
The hon. member asked how many people will use that. The provision is in place for that to happen.
The main thrust of the opposition is that we should not be charging an interest rate on any of the advance payments.
I would like to educate the hon. member. The producers in my riding have come to me and said it is time they started to pick up some of the slack they have been getting for nothing. They are prepared to pay a fair interest rate. What is a fair interest rate? It is prime or lower because it is going to be government guaranteed.
Honourable members over there stand up and tell us to cut spending. They stand up and say: "You have a debt out there that you have increased. You are not doing anything to control these things." They make all of these complaints, but when we attempt to bring things into line in a more equitable way, they stand up and scream because we use closure. We are imposing closure because those very people over there have done absolutely nothing to co-operate and assist.
I have producers in my riding who phone me to ask when this is going to be passed so they can get an advance payment. I tell them to phone the member for Oshawa. I tell them they might get something if they
Government Orders
phone both of those lame duck leaders of the two parties across the way, but I doubt it.
It is unfortunate that the tone of this House and the tone of co-operation has dropped so dramatically over the past three or four years. Sometimes I am ashamed to sit in my seat in this House and watch what goes on. I saw it last night when we in this House wasted time and money for three and a half hours.
The opposition talks about wasting money. We had people on overtime. The pages were here when they should have been home studying. We had all the staff of the House of Commons, the staff in Debates, and all of those areas working overtime because the people across the way wanted to prove a point. They wanted to make us all stand for every single vote.
What did it amount to? We voted from six o'clock until past nine-thirty, three and a half hours, while those members were sitting there trying to embarrass us or prove a point or gain something in principle rather than allow us to go back to our offices to do some work and allow people to go home and be with their families like they should have been. That is the kind of attitude that we are getting in this House and that is the kind of attitude we have been getting since we came back in September.
It is too bad. They are still fighting the last election. Again I point out that I have producers phoning me asking when they can get their advance payment. I am telling them that they can get an advance payment when these amendments go through. These amendments are necessary. These amendments are supported by the vast majority of producers who I have talked to in my riding. They are supporting these amendments because some of them want to access more advance payments and more funds.
Opposition members cannot speak out of both sides of their mouths. They continually do that, but they have got to be taken to task for this.
I am not going to waste the time of the House any longer. I have put on record why we are using closure. We have had absolutely no co-operation from those people over there. It is obvious that they are not going to give us any more co-operation at any other time. I would recommend to this government that if it has to use closure on every single piece of legislation, then that is exactly what it should do because we are not going to get co-operation from those people across the way. They say it is against the law. It is not. I read very clearly into the

Government Orders
record how it is not against the law. It reads very clearly. If hon. members over there want to get a copy of the act, they can read it and understand that it is not against the law.
I said obey the law.

The first discussions took place in late June.
Major discussions started to take place when we came back to this House in September, and they have done nothing but stonewall. They have done nothing but express all the animosity that they felt because of the election, so we could not get this bill into the house. Then they cry about closure. We are a government that cares about the producers in Canada. We are a government that has cared. All we have to do is look at the record. We care for the agricultural community in this country and we are going to continue to do that.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you agree with me. At least you were smiling. I had better not accuse you of that, Mr. Speaker, you are supposed to be impartial.
The facts are clearly on the record. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs

of what? I guess he was alleging some kind of obstruction from this side of the House.
