They say they had to do it, that they had to use closure. Well, I submit that they did not. If they would have just got their act together, if they had just done a better job, they wouldn't need it. Why do we not review the facts? Why do we not review the record? The record is that they put this very valuable program into limbo back last spring when the hon. Minister of Finance brought down the budget. That was the start of this mess.
What happened after that? Despite the fact that the program was put into limbo, despite the fact that there was this threat put over farmers' heads, despite the fact that the farmers were now left in this state of uncertainty, what did government members do? They sat on then-hands and they did nothing. We went through the latter part of the spring, all through the summer and beginning of the fall and they did nothing. Then they brought in a bill, and lo and behold, it was a mess. It was flawed. It was so bad-and this must have been embarrassing, it really must have been humiliating, if they ever do feel humiliation-they had to withdraw it. Right?
Right.

My hon. friend confirms. They had to withdraw the bill. That is the kind of sloppiness that you people carry off. You withdrew the bill and then you brought in this one, Bill C-36. Then you accuse us of

Government Orders
some kind of obstruction. You urge us to get it done. We have to get it done now for the sake of the fanners.
Where were you in May and June? Where were you in July and August, September and October? What were you doing? You certainly were not minding the store. You were not minding your business.
On top of that most farm organizations in this country have stated that it is bad legislation. It is the wrong way to go. Is the government listening? Not on your life. It does not listen. It is going ahead and telling us we have to do it now and please, please stand aside. This is a performance that ought not be repeated.
This program has been in effect for over 40 years. It was brought in by a Conservative government, if my grasp of history is proper. I think the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker would be quite disturbed if he knew what is going on today. He represented a prairie province, a prairie constituency and prairie people. I am not too sure if he would be very excited about this kind of legislation to change legislation that worked well.
I do not know of too many farm organizations that were saying "Gut this program. We certainly do not want cash advances on an interest-free basis, no way". I did not hear prairie farmers or any farmers across the country saying that, not on your life. It was not costing a lot of money, only $26 million or $27 million. In the context of other expenditures, that is not a lot of money.
I think that farmers are a little bewildered by it all because, in effect, the government is saying that it has to reach into their pockets for $27 million. All in the name of deficit reduction to get spending down, the government is going to ask them to make this sacrifice. It is important. The government is asking farmers to make this sacrifice. It just wants another $27 million. Maybe in another world, in other circumstances, farmers would understand.
Farmers are a little bewildered because they know what is going on and they know something about the record. Since this government came to power five years ago, where has spending gone?
When the government came to power in 1984, it was taking in $70 billion in revenues. Now it is taking in $112 billion. Extra revenues amount to $42 billion. That is a pretty good take, a sizeable chunk of money, $42 billion.
The farmers are saying 'You want a little more out of me. You want to just take that extra bit out of me, $27 million". No wonder the farmer is a little bewildered. There is more.
Farmers are asked to make this sacrifice but what is the government doing at the same time? The debt goes up. It never stops going up. If we use the five-year record of the government, when it came to power, the debt was $170 billion. Now it is $350 billion, $360 billion. Little wonder farmers in this country are bewildered when this government comes after them again.
There is another dimension to this burden, shared not by farmers alone but by all Canadians, an increase in taxation. We have said many times in the House how good this government has been at increasing taxes. Perhaps it is another fetish. Thirty-one times this government has raised taxes and there is yet to come the grand-daddy of all, the so-called goods and services tax, the grief and suffering tax, which is going to take another $10 billion out of the pockets of Canadians.
My good friend from Brandon-Souris, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment, has taken his place in the House. He represents what I would call a good slice of God's country. Given the fact that the hon. parliamentary secretary is close to the soil and close to farmers in southwestern Manitoba, I would have thought that if there ever was one on the other side of the House who could talk some sense into this government, to bring to the cabinet a sense of reality, it would be that honourable gentleman. I am sure he has tried but he has failed, and that is too bad.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He's the one they've been listening to.

You may have been listening to him but you have not been listening very well. I think that perhaps you should check your ears.
Another thing that we have to consider in the context of the heavy burden that I just recited is that farmers are also concerned about not only themselves but their entire community, rural Canada, the way this government is closing down rural Canada. There is a litany of complaints about the way the government is treating rural Canada, the way the government is shutting down rural post offices, gutting VIA Rail, closing down mili-
October 26, 1989

tary bases and, of course, doing most of it without any kind of consultation.
What has gone wrong with the process? Is there something demeaning about consulting with Canadians? Is it beneath this government to talk to the farmers? Have things got that bad in Canada?
No wonder the farmers are bewildered. They wonder whether they have any friends in the nation's capital. Look what has happened in the wake of the free trade agreement with respect to certain producers, to supply management, to orderly marketing.
I think it was just a few years ago that we thought that these were solid, secure institutions, that no one would dare dismantle them. I guess maybe we were thinking wrongly. Perhaps we should have been a bit more wary, particularly of this government.
Look what has happened just recently with Durum wheat producers. I thought that we in this country championed success, I thought we applauded success. I thought we always said to the men and women of this country, "Go out and work hard and do well. We want you to succeed, and if you succeed you will be rewarded". I am quite sure the Durum wheat producers in this country followed that dictum, and they have been doing quite well, in fact so well that we now hear complaints from our good friends to the south: "You can't do that, you're succeeding too well. If you don't stop selling so much, if you don't stop being so competitive, well, we may just threaten you with a countervail".
That is pretty disturbing because we know what has happened in other agriculture spheres. Just ask milk producers, egg producers and pork producers. The list goes on and on. Even one of the gentleman closely attached to the free trade negotiations, Mr. Clayton Yeutter, expressed sympathy for the Durum wheat producers in North Dakota, a state of the union just across the border from my province. He said, and it is on record in a letter to the Durum wheat producers of North Dakota, that the Americans might even consider pushing a countervail so that they can put a stop to this rather unseemly competition from north of the border.
What do we hear from the government? Not a heck of a lot. I think we could hear a lot more. We want to hear a lot more.

I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you have put up your famous finger, which signals one minute to go. I would urge my good friends who are chuckling on the other side-maybe they have heard something important this afternoon. Right?
Right.
It is a little late in the debate, but I do sense that government members' ears are opening, that in the last 20 minutes, there has been a little penetration, perhaps just a little. Right?
Right.

Given this penetration, just let me say this. I would urge them to reconsider the bill, withdraw it, consult with farmers and get it right for a change. Get it right for farmers and get it right for the country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why in the last month I have had such a tendency to pick up the remarks of the person who spoke before me. It must be a hold-over from being on a committee or something.
Picking up from my colleague who spoke last, I do not believe that this government is capable of getting anything right. The hon. member also indicated that perhaps there was some measure of understanding breaking through. I despair that that will never happen either. I despair for at least two reasons, the first being that until last May, I was a little more closely connected to the agriculture community than I am now. I sold the quarter section of land I owned at that time, but I would like to establish that I do have connections to the soil having grown up in rural Saskatchewan. In fact, it is almost impossible to be from Saskatchewan and not have some kind of a rural connection. Certainly many of my relatives are still farmers there. I appreciate what they do and I am a part of what they do.
I despair for the second reason in that for the second time in two days, I find myself having to stand against closure. If the message on this bill is not filtering through to the government, I rather suspect that the message is filtering through to the Canadian public that what we have here is a government elected a year ago which really cares not. I guess it is a misnomer to call it a government. It is not governing. The people opposite are ruling. I rather suspect that Good King John would be

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
very proud of the way these people are railroading their way through this Parliament.
King John D.

No, not King John D. King John D. would not be all that pleased about it either. King John would be very pleased with the way these people are ruling. Those of an earlier era who fought so hard to bring in the Magna Carta would be as despairing as I am at the way these people are railroading their way through Parliament.
The agricultural community from one end of this land to the other has nothing very good to say about this piece of legislation. Why on earth would they rush to make use of this when they can go to their banks and get interest rates that are as favourable on loans as this government is giving? Why, when previously they were able to get interest-free loans on the commodities which the agricultural community worked so hard to produce would they be pleased that this legislation is being introduced?
I guess there are other questions which have to be asked in relation to this legislation. One of them certainly is why would the government introduce it. I suspect, in considering the way this government has operated since it was elected in 1984, one of the main reasons that it is being introduced is that what happened previously had the effect, if not directly and formally, of being almost a marketing board. It had a levelling effect on the ability of the producers to be able to realize to the fullest extent possible within certain limitations the fullest value for what they produced.
It meant that they were not forced, in order to have available funds at the end of the growing season when the crops become available, to sell those commodities immediately. They were not forced to glut the market with the things that they produced. Glutting the market would have the effect of lowering prices which may at first blush have been an advantage for the consumers but later on in the year, after the commodities had been used up, after the supply was gone and the prices went up, we would consume in many instances imported products and the prices would have been higher than they ever were. The consumer certainly would not benefit from that.
I suspect that certainly part of the rationale was to get away from something that had the effect of levelling those things out. When prices are relatively level, it does away with speculation. I suspect that there are a good many friends of the government who were only too pleased to be able to get involved in speculation on the commodities which our agricultural producers spend so much time producing. We say the producers ought to be able to benefit to the fullest extent. The interest free cash advance allowed that to happen.
What will happen now will do away with the orderly marketing part of the agricultural community which has been in place for so many years. The same effect will be felt no matter which commodities we are talking about. The relatively orderly marketing, transportation and in-elevator storage of western grains is being severely affected by this foolish action of the government.
Rail line abandonment, of course, is another issue. I suppose there will be some piece of legislation here shortly concerning railways for which we will see a closure motion as well. Nevertheless, over the years with rail line abandonment and the subsequent abandonment of rural elevators, the elevator storage of commodities in western Canada has been severely limited. With the ability farmers had from the advance payment to sell their commodities over a period of time throughout the year, the elevator system, depleted though it was, was not congested.
Likewise, the same could be said of rail transportation of grain throughout the country as well. It had that levelling effect on rail transportation as well as the storage of grain off farm. That is in jeopardy if this legislation goes through.
We can talk about vegetables. One of my colleagues referred to what happens with vegetables. Again, once the harvesting season occurs, there is a flooding of vegetables onto the market with the subsequent lowering of prices which does not occur if there is some kind of advance so that the farmer can get some kind of a stabilization of his income throughout the year to be able to pay off some of his debts in a more orderly way.
If it comes to a point where the farmer is forced to sell his vegetables at a lower price than ought to be realized and the stabilization program kicks in, in all probability, not only will the cost to the government through the stabilization plan be more than the support for the interest rate, it will also put into place the possibility of
October 26, 1989

the Americans bringing in a countervailing action because of this stabilization program itself. That is another one of the dangers that is most likely to occur as a result of bringing in this kind of legislation.
There have been some references to the fact that the Opposition is holding up this legislation. This is not so. There is nothing now to prevent the government from giving advance payments to the agricultural community under the present legislation. The government has simply decided not to make cash advances under the present legislation. I do not know whether it is trying to punish the Opposition or whether it is trying to punish the farmer, but whatever the case may be, it certainly is not the Opposition's fault that the farmers have been unable to get cash advances.
I see that my time has pretty well run out. I thank you very much for the opportunity to have spoken on this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on a motion focusing on the needs of children and on effective ways to better ensure that Canadian children live in a happy, safe and secure environment. Clearly all of us care about our children
Private Members' Business
and see the future in terms of the life circumstances of these children.
Today I would like to focus on one of the key problems facing society, one which is having grave, long-lasting effects on our children, and that is the problem of family violence. To call the violence that is occurring within many Canadian families a phenomenon is perhaps not quite appropriate. For children, women and men trapped in the vicious cycle of family violence, it is a hard and frightening day-to-day reality. For those of us who remember our childhood fondly and continue to be enriched by our family lives, it is hard to imagine the family as anything other than a source of our greatest comfort, happiness and love.
In the past decade, a number of studies have been commissioned by governments or professional organizations that have provided new information and startling statistics about the incidents of family violence that challenge our most basic assumptions about what is really going on inside many Canadian families. These statistics in particular have grabbed headlines and national attention.
In 1980, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women reported that one in 10 women were beaten on a regular basis by their husbands or partners. In 1987, a follow-up report said an estimated one million Canadian women were being battered by the men with whom they live.
Professor Robin Badgley told us one in two young women experience some kind of sexual abuse during their childhood as do one in three young men. In fact, Badgley told us that 42 per cent of our population were victims of unwanted sexual acts at some point in their lives.
Only a few years ago the Fraser report on the incidence of prostitution shocked us further with the statistics on juvenile prostitution. The Canadian Centre for Justice Statistics reported that in 1986, 191 homicides, or 40 per cent of all homicides that year, involved people who were either related by blood or marriage or lived in a common law situation. It is hard to believe, I am sure. In response, governments and communities across the

October 26, 1989
Private Members' Business
country have developed a wide range of programs and services in support of families dealing with violence.
Most notably, over the last decade a significant number of crisis centres have opened, most recently as a result of the federal government's Project Haven. Likewise, progress has been made in areas of police intervention and their policy of laying assault charges against those who abuse their spouses. As well, a number of media campaigns and public service announcements have served to increase our awareness of the problem.
This government introduced and passed new legislation a couple of years ago which makes it easier for children to testify in sexual abuse cases. Mr. Rix Rogers, well known for his work on behalf of the voluntary sector, was appointed as a special adviser to the Minister of National Health and Welfare on child sexual abuse. And, as we have already heard, Mr. Rogers is expected to present his report to the minister.
For many years, the federal government has shared with the provinces the cost of crisis intervention programs and through the Canada Assistance Plan, the provision of shelters in communities across the land. We have also done our part to co-ordinate and collect information for services providers and researchers through the National Clearinghouse on Family Violence. In addition, the federal government has funded a large number of projects and studies and has been at the table for nearly every discussion of substance on family violence that has taken place in the past decade.
Internationally, as well, Canada is well known for the priority it gives to the prevention of family violence. For example, in the mid-1980s Canada put family violence on the agenda of a European meeting of ministers responsible for social affairs. The Canadian government has also made a major statement to the United Nations inter-regional consultation on social welfare which asserted that family violence should be a concern in all societies, regardless of culture, age, or economic status. As we all know, Canada is also very much involved in the United Nations activity on the Convention of the Rights of the Child, which is expected to be adopted later this year.
Though we have plenty to be proud of, we would all be kidding ourselves to think we are even close to finding solutions which get to the root of the problem. There are a few things of which we can be sure. We know the cost to our society is great in personal and global societal terms. We know many of our costly social programs are rooted in violence which begins at home. We also know that family violence tends to be passed on from generation to generation. The little girl abused by her father all too often becomes a battered wife or turns to prostitution. The young man who watched his father dominate his mother with violence learns to repeat that pattern with his own family.
Our penitentiaries, our hospitals, our schools, our transition houses, our streets, are full of people who have learned first hand the lesson taught by violence. Other lessons about civility, personal and social responsibility, and trust come much harder. We know too that it is usually when we combine our resources that we collectively move closer to finding real solutions to family violence.
In its report "Battered but not Beaten", the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women gave all the service providers active in the violence area a pat on the back for the work they have done to date. The report's author said, however, that despite all our good intentions and good work we had a fundamental problem, our efforts failed the "reality test". The author says we just did not always meet the test of the battered individual's reality. We do not always understand, nor are we always equipped to address the real human needs, either before or after the violence occurs. It is at the individual "people" level where the hurt lingers and where the answers must be found.
It is also at the individual "people" level that families come into play. While families are the source of hurt for some, they can become the source of comfort for others. We all certainly have to recognize the essentialness of the family.
But where do we go from there? We certainly cannot stand by and watch the violence continue. In the ideal world I think we all want to move closer to the positive vision of the family. We all want to see a safe place to call our own. We all want to have children and spouses nearby to enjoy time together. We all want to be secure
October 26, 1989

in our relations, to be free of fear, to have a sense of well-being that comes with security of hearth and home, to be cared about.
The federal government alone cannot deliver that perfect vision of the future to individual Canadians. The causes and effects of family violence are much too complex for us to presume so much. Only through a partnership with the provincial governments, the voluntary sector, service providers and, most importantly, communities across the country, can we have a good chance of restoring some balance and some security to those who have lived with violence.
The federal government has already called on this partnership, on this co-operative effort, most recently, of course, in the form of National Health and Welfare's announcement yesterday to pledge financial support of up to $1.3 million for the "Kids Help Line".
As you may know, the Kids Help Line was launched by the Canadian Children's Foundation in May, 1989. It offers immediate, free and anonymous help to Canada's seven million children. Counselling, information and, if appropriate, referral services are provided to children and youth experiencing a variety of problems including child abuse and/or neglect, loneliness, alcohol or substance abuse.
Federal moneys will be available over the next 12-month period. Six hundred and fifty thousand of the $1.3 million will be provided immediately and the remainder will be made available on the basis of a dollar-for-dollar matching with financial support from other sources, most importantly, the corporate sector.
We have made a lot of progress, but there is clearly much more work to be done. This government takes this issue and this challenge very seriously and will continue to strive to foster a society that is caring and secure.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak as strongly and as passionately as I can in support of this motion.
In legislation in various jurisdictions across this country that relates to the family there is a phrase that recurs over and over again. That phrase is, "The best interests of the child are paramount". We see that phrase in federal and provincial legislation. We hear lip service paid to it on almost a daily basis by lawyers, social
Private Members' Business
workers and judges, by people in this country generally. The problem is that that is all it is, it is lip service.
In Canada in 1989 the status of the child, of far too many children, is one of poverty, of fear, of abuse. One million children or more in this country live in poverty. One million children or more in this country have to depend for their sustenance upon food banks. Children in every province and territory of this country are subject to horrendous forms of abuse that would give nightmares, and do give nightmares, to any one of us sitting in this House.
The problem is that we all, as a group, agree that this situation must stop, that children need to be protected, that if we have no other task to accomplish, not as politicians or legislators, but as human beings, the protection of our children has to be the foremost action to be taken in our lives.
The kinds of things to which children have a right crop up in legislation right across the country. As well, one of the areas of reference for a motion such as this is the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. That particular document talks about a child's right to care, a child's right to a home, to adequate health care, to protection from abuse, to protection from exploitation and to protection from war. Obviously, there are things that we can do about this in the short term and things that we can do about it in the long term. But the blot on the escutcheon of every one of us as Canadians, is that we do very little about it at all.
Every day in this country social workers, school nurses, teachers, lawyers, all sorts of different levels of professionals who work in the area of children's rights, see time and again how the system prevents us from adequately protecting children.
Just recently we have heard terrible stories of sexual abuse. It is not limited to one province, it is not limited to one neighbourhood. It goes on everywhere. It is not limited to a particular social or economic class. It is not limited to a particular geographic area. And what do we do in response? We sit back and say, "This is terrible, something must be done".
In supporting this motion we see the opportunity to actually do something. This is not something that depends on partisan politics. I do not think there is a soul in this House that would not rise to fight for the rights of defenceless children. But the time has come for action. As my colleague across the way said, it can only be done in co-operation with the provinces. But, the political will, I suggest, must come from the federal government

October 26, 1989
Private Members' Business
to make the move to the various provinces. The support that is necessary to get programs and legislation such as this, in its various forms, where it is necessary in the different jurisdictions off the ground, has to have a prime mover and that prime mover should be the federal government.
Every day when we hear about the various problems besetting children across this country there seems to be one or more that will take the limelight for a short period of time. Not to denigrate the need for action and positive support- in the area of child sexual abuse, or in the area of physical abuse against children generally, I think that we have to look at this in a more cosmic manner, if you will. We have to look at the very basics that are necessary for children-not even necessary, but that are the rights of children. We have to look at the need for shelter, proper nutrition, proper schooling and proper health care.
I mentioned earlier the various workers who toil on a daily basis against overwhelming odds to assist children. One particular experience that I had as a practising lawyer comes to mind. It was the case of two children who were apprehended because they were, indeed, children in need of protection. They were in the custody of a parent who had a severe alcohol problem and who was absolutely incapable of caring for them. The two children were apprehended by the relevant authority. They were approximately three years apart in age. One child was placed in a foster home, the other child was placed in a group home. The foster home and the group home were 40 miles apart, there was no opportunity for these two children to see each other and to maintain almost the only form of emotional contact and emotional relationship that had sustained them in their short lives.
The younger child became very withdrawn. Again, the social workers were worried, the judge was concerned, the lawyers were concerned. Everybody was worried but there was no facility available to keep these two siblings in the same place. Finally, after a tremendous effort by all concerned, after three months a foster home that would take both children was found. I can only speculate
as to the damage that had been done in this length of time to two already damaged children.
In a sense it was nobody's fault in the specific. It was not the judge's fault, the lawyers' or the social workers' fault. It was the lack of a political will to provide the atmosphere for children in need of protection, to ensure that in attempting to protect them we do not worsen their situation. It is not cheap and it is not easy, but it is the major duty of all of us to provide it.
A further thing that took place, indeed with these same children, was the realization by all the professionals involved in this particularly tragic case of the relationship between the older child and his parent. It had become a reversal of the parent-child relationship. This child was taking the responsibility and ran away on various occasions from the group home because he felt he had the responsibility to care for his alcoholic parent. This child was 11 years old.
Because of the lack of support services for this family from the beginning of its troubles, because of the lack of emotional support, the lack of counselling, and just the general lack of a plan to deal with children who are suffering in our society, this child became delinquent and eventually ended up in the young offenders system in our courts.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the member for Mission-Coquitlam for bringing forward this motion. I would like to utter un cri de coeur to all of us here in this House that when it comes to the issue of children and their needs and their rights that we put aside our partisan considerations and work as a single unit to bring about the legislative and social support systems that are needed to ensure that children can take their full place and receive their rightful heritage in our country.

I am
pleased to have the opportunity to speak to this motion presented by my colleague for Mission-Coquitlam. I am pleased to be able to support this motion.
This comes at a very critical time for it is long past the time that we took the issue of children's welfare seriously. Society has developed many altruistic and benign phrases with regards to children. We have all used expressions such as, "children are our greatest resource"
October 26, 1989

or "children are our future". These words are correct because children are our future, they are our greatest resource, and they are presently the ones who we as a society have failed most harshly.
The United Nations General Assembly has been grappling with the issue of children's rights for the past three decades. Ten years ago it established the International Year of the Child. Now, after years of consultation and negotiation, the General Assembly is going to, hopefully, adopt a convention on the rights of the child.
It is imperative that we address this situation nationally and internationally for the problems affecting children are critical. Throughout the world children bear the brunt of society's callousness, whether it is through war, poverty or the lack of status within their own country. We know that there have been over 200 wars since the end of World War II. With the advent of technology we have all been able to see images of never-ending armed conflict in our world.
We have seen a young girl run from the horror of a napalm attack. We have all seen toddlers picking their way through the rubble of Beruit. In a really haunting photo we have seen an infant held in his father's arms dead after a poison gas attack. War has made them orphans. It has turned them into refugees. Indeed, over half of the world's 12 to 14 million refugees are children. We know the many problems that refugees face; overcrowded camps, long waiting lists for entry into safe countries. However the situation is much worse for children who are refugees. Should they be fortunate enough to escape to an area of greater peace, the future for them is still very bleak.
The United Nations estimates that almost 100 million children today are homeless. Their only means of survival is on the street. This means that they have no personal security and no adequate source of nutrition. Many of them are unable to receive even a basic level of education. It is estimated that one-seventh of all school age boys in the world are unable to attend school, and the situation is much worse for school age girls, Mr. Speaker. One-quarter of these girls are not in school. Many of them are not in school because they are forced into the workforce. Child labour is a booming activity around our
Private Members' Business
world. Over 80 million children between the ages of 10 and 14 are working, and this figure increases once we add in those children under the age of 10.
If the statistics about war and homelessness and poverty are not bad enough, we should take a moment to look at the bottom line of our treatment of children. Forty thousand children die each and every day from starvation, from polluted water and from disease in our world. Each one of these 40,000 deaths could be prevented by one single vaccination. Could anything be so simple? Can anything be as cruel to deny this?
We can prevent these unnecessary deaths. To give everyone in the world; women, men and children, adequate health, food, shelter and education would cost only $17 billion. For anyone who thinks that this is an outrageous figure, Mr. Speaker, let me put it in relative terms. Every two weeks the world spends that much money on weapons alone.
I know that everyone in this House is disturbed by such negligence towards innocent children, but this problem is not a problem restricted to only the poorest of nations or to those countries that are plagued by civil war. The problems are also reaching crisis proportions here in Canada. Today, here in Canada, one in five children live in poverty. For many of us that is a very frightening statistic, but for over one million children in Canada that is the debilitating reality.
To be a child bom into a poor family in Canada today is to have a death rate that is 50 per cent to 100 per cent higher than that of children bom into affluent families. If these children are fortunate enough to survive they will experience more health problems. The disadvantages continue as they grow older as poor children are twice as likely to drop out of school.
This problem is approaching epidemic proportions, but why? Because we are forcing more and more of our children into poverty. The Canadian Council on Social Development has recently issued the Canadian Fact Book on Poverty. It notes that in 1975 someone who was receiving minimum wage and supporting a spouse and a child earned an income equivalent to 81 per cent of the poverty line. By 1986 the same worker earned only 46 per cent of the poverty line. Now, with both spouses working for minimum wage, they would still reach only 92 percent of the poverty line.

October 26, 1989
Private Members' Business
Our present system entrenches these individuals into a life of poverty, and it is the children who are the most harmed. In Canada 61.8 per cent of children of single mothers live in poverty. In Sweden the figure is only 9.8 per cent. We do have options that are available to us. Unfortunately, our government refuses to act.
First of all, present rates of social assistance fail to provide any real semblance of fair support. The Social Planning and Research Council has noted that in my own home province of British Columbia assistance rates are far from realistic. On B.C. welfare rates a parent is only able to feed a child properly, using the Canada Food Guide, for two and a half weeks out of every month. What are these children expected to eat for the following 12 days? Malnourished and hungry children are unable to function properly in school. Some schools now offer a lunch program to battle the growing problem of hungry children.
I recently visited a school in Vancouver, one of only five schools in the whole city of Vancouver, that offers a hot lunch program to children. It is a great deal of work for the parents in that community, for the teachers and the support staff, but it is wonderful to watch these little children carrying their trays up to receive a nutritious meal at lunch time.
What are we doing to help all the other children in Canada who fall between the cracks of our social assistance programs? Unfortunately, if the government continues with its present agenda, the situation will only worsen.
This government has not raised the federal minimum wage since 1986. At $4 an hour it still remains the lowest minimum wage in all of Canada. We have not developed any cohesive and responsible system of job creation. Three-fifths of the jobs created in the last four years have been low-wage jobs. The government is reinforcing the chains of poverty on children.
If the federal government is truly committed to protecting children it will act. The government has a choice. It can continue to address the needs of big business or it can look at the faces of the children who are lined up at food banks, crowded into unsanitary, unsafe housing, and say, "Enough is enough".
I support this bill, and I congratulate my colleague for Mission-Coquitlam for bringing it forward.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to start the debate on Motion No. 254, in the name of the Hon. Member for Mission-Coquitlam (Ms. Langan), with a quote from the Grand dictionnaire des citations frangaises by Collange which reads as follows: "Children can teach us to take advantage of every moment instead of complaining about the weather".
I thought this was very apt, Mr. Speaker. As the father of two children, I agree that having children is truly an enjoyable experience. You know, sometimes when you come home and you see toys all over the place, you sigh: They haven't put them away yet. And you complain.
However, Mr. Speaker, when you think about it, you are glad those toys are there, because it means the house is alive, and you realize it is nice to have a family.
To get back to motion No. 254 in the name of the hon. member whom I got to know a little better when she travelled with us across the country when the committee was considering Bill C-21 on unemployment insurance reform-she is a very dedicated person and I understand why she is anxious to have a special bill of rights that will protect children.
We are talking about missing children, children who have been abused, about violence against children and also about sexual abuse.
Mr. Speaker, in this connection I would like to mention that the Ministry of the Solicitor General has played an important national role in responding to the missing children issues.
Before providing the details on current ministry involvement in missing children, it may be useful to recall the history of the federal government's involvements in the issue.
In 1985 the government was faced with growing public concern about child abductions by strangers.
Public concerns were based on a small number of well publicized cases of the abduction and murder of children. These public concerns were intensified by alarmist and inaccurate media reports.
October 26, 1989

At the time, reliable national statistics were not available in Canada to put these concerns in perspective, by providing accurate information on the actual extent of the problem in Canada. In response to this situation, the then Solicitor General of Canada, announced a missing children initiative in December, 1985. As key elements of this initiative, the minister announced plans for a national forum on missing children, the creation of a missing children registry within the RCMP and initiated a research program on missing children.
The overall objective of these initiatives was to increase our knowledge of the problem and of the needs of missing children, and to use that knowledege as the basis for a concerted national effort to improve efforts to prevent children going missing, and secondly to improve the overall responses of police, government departments, social agencies, and voluntary groups in locating and helping missing children.
As you know, the police are normally the lead community agency in responding to a missing child incident. This is true whether the child has run away from his or her home, been abducted by a parent or abducted by a stranger.
The creation of the RCMP Missing Children Registry, in July, 1986, has been the single most important contribution of the Ministry of the Solicitor General to the missing children issue.
The centre has a direct link to the missing persons file of the Canadian Police Information Centre. Whenever a missing child is reported to a police agency in any part of Canada, this report is immediately entered in the C.P.I.C. missing persons file.
Thanks to direct access to the missing children files, the registry staff is able to assist the efforts of police agencies, provincial government departments, social agencies and organizations such as Child Find to locate and return missing children.
The registry's statistics demonstrate both the magnitude of the missing children problem in Canada, and the importance of the role of the registry and the police in responding.
Thus registry statistics for 1987 show that over 57,000 missing children incidents were reported to Canadian
Private Members' Business
police, and that in 56,000 of the incidents, the children were located during that same period. At any given time, there are approximately 1,500 children currently missing and reported to Canadian police. This is not a negligible figure, 1,500 children missing at any given time.
The registry staff play an important role in international liaison. For example, registry staff assist United States jurisdictions searching for missing children in Canada. They also help Canadian agencies contact the appropriate jurisdictions in the United States in searching for missing children believed to be in the U.S. To ensure effective international co-ordination of efforts to locate and return missing children, the registry maintains contact with the U.S. state and federal clearing houses for missing children, as well as with Interpol, External Affairs, Canada Customs, and voluntary agencies.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the RCMP-and Canadian police agencies from coast to coast-deserve high praise for the manner in which they have responded to the needs of missing children. You can imagine how hard it must be on a family!
In addition to the creation of the RCMP Missing Children's Registry, the Ministry of the Solicitor General has undertaken a program of research on assessing children in four major police agencies-Montreal, Toronto, Edmonton and Surrey, B.C. The purpose of the study was to understand the nature of the problem including the relationship with other social ills including family violence, child abuse and delinquency.
The findings of the research reinforce the statistics from the missing children's registry. The majority of the missing children incidents reported to the police involve children running from their home or from an institution. Many of these children run away more than once during the same year. After runaways, abductions by parents constitute the second largest category of missing children incidents reported to the police. Abductions by strangers constitue a smaller but nevertheless important number of cases. Such abductions are most serious and difficult to live with for the families.
These findings, as well as the experience of the missing children's registry, underline the fact that all missing children should be considered at risk. Whether the child is fleeing an unhealthy family environment or has been abducted by a parent in the context of a custody dispute-and certainly when abducted by a stranger-

Private Members' Business
the child's intellectual, emotional and moral development and physical safety is threatened.
Mr. Speaker, our Department will also continue to cooperate with other federal departments, provincial governments and voluntary agencies in the search for effective preventive and support networks for missing children, and indeed for all children and young people who need help.
Mr. Speaker, in our colleague's Motion 254, she wants a children's emergency hotline established. You know that there is a voluntary organization, the Canadian Children's Foundation, which has already set this up. Since May this year, it has operated the first emergency telephone line for Canadian children. It is called Kid's Help Phone and provides some seven million children with immediate, free, anonymous assistance, in both languages.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the positive results achieved, with some 654 phone calls a day or 45,000 cases in the last few months, our Government will spend $1.3 million in a 12-month period to support the work that has been done by this agency and to ensure that there will always be a telephone line to help children going through difficult times, whether due to sexual abuse or something else.

Mr. Speaker, in listening to the comments of the previous speaker, I have to concur that, yes, there have been some initiatives made by the federal Department of National Health and Welfare with regard to children. However, in reading the motion as put forward by my colleague from Mission-Coquitlam, it states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize the laws throughout the country-
What could be so wrong with that particular submission? It goes on to state that that bill of rights ought to include a child protection commission, and an emergency hotline. I cannot understand how any member on any side of this particular Chamber could object to the substance or, more particularly, to the intent of the motion as put forward by my colleague.
It is very clear that what is being suggested in this motion is something that all parliamentarians, regardless of political persuasion, ought to support. Yes, there may be some fine tuning from time to time that members opposite would wish to include, add or amend, but the intent is very clear.
The third part of the motion it talks about an emergency hotline. We are all aware that very recently the Canadian Children's Foundation, a national non-profit fund raising organization put together what is known as the Kids Hotline. Yes, the government has participated to a certain extent, but the government also now knows that this national organization is in need of federal funding. It would not an ongoing expense of the Government of Canada, but a one-time grant to be given to that organization so that it may carry on its activities.
What the hon. member is suggesting in her motion is before the Canadian people at the present time. I assume all of us who are sincere when we say we wish to do things for and on behalf of children must conclude this motion is acceptable in terms of form, acceptable in terms of its intent, and acceptable in terms of its substance.
A U.S. child psychologist said, and I quote: "The concept of childhood is threatened with extinction in the society we have created. Today's child has become the unwilling, unintended victim of overwhelming stress, the stress born by rapid bewildering social change and constantly rising expectations."
In our rapid, fast-moving society, we have made great strides when it comes to technology and dealing with changing labour market demands. As with most strides or progress made in one field, another field usually gets left behind. Unfortunately, the children of the world and, yes, the children of our country, have been subject to this oversight.
One could argue with very little difficulty that the children have been robbed of their childhood. Children need time to grow, to learn, to laugh and, yes, to feel free. Society today, however, has laboured our children with social problems that serve only to stunt their growth and their development. To name a few there is child abuse, sexual abuse, child suicide, runaways, kidnapping, neglect, child pornography, child prostitution, emotional
October 26, 1989

and psychological developments, drug and alcohol abuse, child crimes and teenage pregnancy.
As all hon. members would attest, the children of the 1980s and 1990s are not the same as the children of the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s. Today, a child is told not to talk to strangers, not to take candy from strangers, not to be left alone with a teacher or, indeed, anyone else. It could be argued-and I argue it-that we have a generation of children growing up and learning not to trust. This is very sad. It is very sad for parents, very sad for institutions which must deal with children and, yes, very sad for the children themselves.
It is our fault as Canadians, because their trust has been violated. One prime obvious sad travesty is a situation which we have all evidenced on national television, that being the situation in the province of Newfoundland.
We thought it was only adults who experienced stress and anxiety. Children have been diagnosed with free-floating anxiety. In adolescence, free-floating anxiety can take the form of depression and contribute to suicide. In Toronto, as in many large cities, the increase in stress reactions among young people have been so great that special children and adolescent services have been set up to care for these youngsters.
A clinical psychologist, Diane Syer, who is at the crisis intervention unit at the Toronto East General Hospital, said, "This trend can be blamed on the fragmentation of the family and the erosion of social institutions such as religion, the mobility of people in our society and a pervasive sense that the future will be grim."
All children have special needs, intellectual, social and emotional. These needs are not necessarily the same as adults. Children do not learn and think in the same way as adults. For these reasons alone we need a comprehensive bill of rights for children.
When all else has been told, the best years of your life are when you are young. For many children there is truth in this statement, but for many others that is not the truth. We need a bill of rights for children to protect children by law and to bring back the real meaning of childhood.
The institutions of the 1940s and 1950s, indeed the 1960s and part of the 1970s, in many instances no longer serve our children the way they ought to. There is a role, a fiduciary obligation if you will or a moral obligation on the state, namely the national government, to provide
Private Members' Business
leadership in an important area affecting children across this land.
I am fully aware, as is I believe my colleague who moved this motion, of the jurisdictional difficulties. Are we as parliamentarians prepared to say that because of the constitutional dilemma that this may present we will not act in the paramount interest of children? Is that what we as a Parliament in 1989-90 wish to say to those children across this land? Surely, if one examines the intent of the motion, the words used are: "the advisability of negotiating with the provinces".
Surely the minister responsible, either the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Solicitor General or indeed the Minister of Justice, would want to put a position paper before the provinces in this country to have them respond, not in a partisan way, but in a very caring, sensitive way, to a Canadian bill of rights for children.
If that were done, if that leadership were exercised by the Government of Canada, I am reasonably confident that the spirit in which it would be made would be one of non-partisanship, one to address children of all ages, of all regions, of all faiths, of all ethnic backgrounds. I am sure you would find in the provinces a sense and a warming to the concept of a bill of rights and thereafter a consensus for its establishment into law under federal statute affecting each and every province.
On that note, keeping in mind that my time is limited, let me congratulate once again my colleague for the introduction of this Private Members' Motion, and to say to all members on both sides that the intent, the form and the substance is something which all members should rise in their place and fully support as it speaks to the best interest of tomorrow's leaders, namely, the young children of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, there are many children in Bourassa, which is why I am delighted with this opportunity to speak to the subject of child welfare once again. I want to thank the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam and the hon. member who spoke earlier for presenting and addressing a motion on the important subject of children's rights and how they should be protected. I think the Hon. member

October 26, 1989
Private Members' Business
will agree that what I have to say may be a satisfactory response to her concerns.
According to the motion tabled in the House:
- the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and this Bill of Rights include a child protection commission,-
Mr. Speaker, this motion faces some very real obstacles in the division of legislative powers provided by our Constitution in this country. We believe, however, that there is a more realistic approach to achieving the objectives expressed in the motion, without changing the division of powers or perhaps disrupting child protection services already in place.
In fact, the solution I intend to propose would make it possible for all parties to go beyond the objectives stated implicitly by the hon. member in her motion.
Mr. Speaker, to ensure that the interests of Canadian children are served as well as possible, the Government of Canada should consider, in close consultation with the provinces and territories, ratifying a draft international agreement designed specifically to protect the rights of the child, not only in Canada but throughout the world. I am, of course, referring to the draft United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which will probably be approved by the UN General Assembly later this year.
The Convention on the Rights of the Child proposed by the United Nations would establish a modern, international standard for the protection of the child's social, economic, political, religious, cultural and civic rights. We are talking about a convention that provides for the widest possible range of rights. Its 54 articles, which are still at the draft stage and concern the rights of the child, guarantee the protection of children without families, children exposed to violence and neglect, children who are the victims of exploitation, whatever form it may take, and handicapped children and their right to be treated without discrimination. By providing for such a wide range of rights for the child, the draft United Nations Convention is a fully satisfactory response to that part of the motion before the House which mentions the need for a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children.
Mr. Speaker, the Convention on the Rights of the Child proposed by the United Nations also provides for a number of mechanisms to monitor compliance. First of all, each country that ratifies the convention shall submit to the United Nations, within two years following ratification, a progress report detailing the nature and scope of the measures taken to implement the provisions of the convention. Furthermore, the draft convention provides for a committee on the rights of the child, an international panel of experts that will be responsible for evaluating the living conditions of children in the countries that ratify the convention. The committee will have the right to publish the results of its inquiries and to recommend certain measures for the protection of children.
If Canada decides to ratify the convention, the Government of Canada would be subject to the same scrutiny as the other signatories.
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the draft UN convention that provide for monitoring the rights of the child will achieve the same objectives or objectives similar to those of the child protection commission proposed by the hon. member.
The UN Convention of the Rights of the Child is receiving more and more support throughout the world. Supporters of the convention have agreed on 1989 as their target year for ratification of the convention by the UN General Assembly. The House will recall that 1989 marks the 10th anniversary of the International Year of the Child as well as the 30th anniversary of the Declaration of the Rights of the Child at the United Nations.
This declaration contains recommendations for the rights of the child but does not have force of law. Unlike the proposed convention, the UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child is not an international legislative instrument that is final and binding.
Mr. Speaker, except for unforeseen circumstances, it is expected that the UN General Assembly will approve the international convention in 1989, so that the Government of Canada will be able to ratify it.
Hon. members will be interested to know that Canada is internationally recognized as having played a leading role in drafting the proposed convention. All or part of versions prepared by Canada were used as the basis for articles on child sexual abuse, health, standard of living,
October 26, 1989

education goals, recreation, economic exploitation, criminal procedure and care mechanisms.
This is just one more reason why the Government of Canada, with the assistance of the provinces and the territories, should consider ratifying the convention.
Mr. Speaker, ratifying the international convention would involve making our laws conform to the convention, both federally and provincially. Since we would be obliged to align our legislation with the provisions of the proposed convention, the ultimate goal of the ratification process would be to provide for some standardization in the provisions of child protection and child welfare legislation across Canada.
To that extent, Mr. Speaker, ratification of the convention would be a response to that part of the motion tabled by the hon. member which asks that child protection laws be standardized across Canada.
Harmonizing federal and provincial legislation with the standards set forth in the proposed UN Convention on the Rights of the Child has been in the works for quite sometime. It is therefore not unlikely that the convention's provisions will be approved by all Canadian jurisdictions.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed convention stresses the right of the child to receive the best possible health care and requires countries to ensure that no child is deprived of access to such care. That is also, Mr. Speaker, the objective pursued by the Government of Canada.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan, the Government of Canada shares with the provinces the cost of helping families who are, or are likely to be, in need and who have children. Family allowances and The Child Tax Credit are among the many other measures designed to afford economic protection to Canadian children.
By definition, children depend on their families, on care-givers or on other adults to whose care they have been entrusted, all of whom must consider the best interests of the child and act accordingly. When that is not the case or worse, when the child is abused or neglected, the child is in danger and something must be done.
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to fight problems like violence against children. We have to make the best interests of the child our priority.
Government Orders
Particular emphasis is placed on the fight against child abuse in the Canadian children's program which is co-ordinated by the Family Violence Prevention Division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The Division is responsible for $20 million in funding for innovative projects that will help prevent child sexual abuse.
The Family Violence Prevention Division was created in 1986 as a visible agency for co-ordinating federal initiatives in the fight against family violence. It includes the National Clearinghouse on Family Violence, a source of information and public awareness tool, thanks to its publications and audio-visual material.
Mr. Speaker, although the merits of the motion before the House are quite obvious, we feel there is a better way to protect the rights of all children.
