Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to rise this afternoon in this Chamber and speak on behalf of every farmer in this country who will be hard done by as a result of the actions of the government in reducing their interest in the rebate of $27 million on their advance payments quota.

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
Before I get into the substance of my remarks, I would like to discuss the comments of my friend for Mackenzie who spoke earlier in the day. I was very interested in his comments, especially those that originally went over some of our heads, when he was talking about his province of Saskatchewan and he mentioned "divine " wisdom and all of those events that happened in the province of Saskatchewan that are led by the "divine" intervention, I would imagine, of the premier of that province.
Also, I cannot help but remark on the comments made by the member for Athabasca who was trying to justify this government's moves in respect to the closure motion. He said that we were the members in this House who were causing the farmers to be denied the benefits to which they were entitled. I feel offended by those comments, inasmuch as I never heard anything that was further removed from the truth.
Since I have been a member of this House, I have seen many instances where the government has done things that it wanted to do without coming to this House for approval. It spent funds without coming to this House for approval. It spent approximately $10 million on advertising the goods and services tax in newspapers right across this country, and it did not come to this House for approval. Yet, the member for Athabasca rises and states that we are denying the farmers in this country the wherewithal to meet their interest commitments. That is not quite correct. I want to draw his attention to that matter.
This government, by its actions, has proven that it does almost anything it wants to do, almost to the point that it has forgotten what the parliamentary system is all about. From our experience, it looks as if it is operating an executive form of government, much the same as our friends in the United States. It seems to be able to do whatever it wants and then come to Parliament for approval after the fact.
The government seems to forget that in the parliamentary system, matters of great concern to this country come before this House, this Chamber for full debate, and once they are debated to their fullest extent, there is a vote. That is the parliamentary system under which this country has operated since 1867, and I suspect will
continue to operate, regardless of what the government is doing with respect to the executive type of administration that it seems to be leading this country into.
As I discuss this executive form of government and its actions, I want to comment on the closure motion. I think this is the ninth time in the short history of this government that it has invoked the time element on the debate of a bill. It is important for us to understand what is happening, particularly when it affects the agricultural community of our country.
Limiting debate is repugnant. It shows an irreverence for this House and a disrespect for its procedures and those things that we, as parliamentarians, have come to hold very dear to our hearts. We hope that by expressing our concerns members opposite would reconsider their future actions and decide that closing debate on vital issues that affect every person is not the proper way to run a country. We have to form a consensus of opinion that meets the needs of the people in this country for the purposes of unity and harmony, and that is what I think we are all trying to achieve.
It does not surprise us that they would move in that direction, inasmuch as this government with this bill on agriculture and its effect on the farmers in our community has shown a complete disrespect for all small town Canada, and rural Canada. This morning we attended a transportation hearing. We were talking about VIA Rail and Rural Dignify made a presentation. When you consider all of the facets that happen in rural Canada today such as the disbanding of rural post offices, the disbanding of passenger rail service in our country, all the other elements that do not affect the cities of Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver, you can see why they would form this allegiance to the big centres of the country and have a complete disregard for our small communities where most of the farmers in our country reside.
When you speak of agriculture in our country your mind wanders immediately. I am from Ontario. When you travel down highway 401 from Toronto to Windsor you can see all those magnificent fields laden with com, black earth and the vegetables that they grow. These lands provide Canadians with fruits and vegetables. These farmers are being hurt by what this government is trying to do with this bill.
October 26, 1989

Government Orders
As your mind wanders and travels to the west, to the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and those magnificent fields of grain, soybeans, and other crops grown there, you think of the crops that are so vital to our communities and to our country. As you think of the grain in the west, you think of the very complex growing system and manufacturing system that we require to grow that grain and get it to those very vital export markets on which we rely to balance our payments.
It is a complex system, and I want to address that in a few moments to show why the farmers in this country need that $27 million in order to make sure that the process is kept in place. When you think of this magnificent industry growing in the western provinces and the subsidies that are required to assist it, and the $27 million is part of that, when you think of the system that is required to take this grain from its source of supply on the farms of this country and trucked to smaller elevators and from the smaller elevators put in the rail cars and shipped, you think immediately of the complex nature of the transportation system that is required.
When you think of transportation and the movement of grain, you automatically think of the Western Grain Transportation Act, and let me just comment on that for a moment. When we talk about agriculture and grain, we cannot help but mention and address the issue of the Western Grain Transportation Act and the inequities that arise out of that particular piece of legislation.
On the one hand, we are talking about $27 million in interest payments, but when you discuss the Western Grain Transportation Act you are not talking of a subsidy on transportation of $550 million or $600 million. I think the numbers that we looked at at the end of last year were well over $1.1 billion in subsidies for the movement of grain in this country from the western provinces to Prince Rupert and Vancouver in British Columbia, or the alternate route in my riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon.
When you consider the enormous subsidy in this western grain transportation program and compare it to the $27 million, it pales by comparison. That Western Grain Transportation Act has to be changed for the benefit of the agricultural producers and for the farmers of this country who are growing our grain, but that is an argument for another day.
We rise in this House on this side to provide support and interest in the hope that we can convince this government to retain the steady and even flow of products into our system.
The system that I talked about is the operative word. In the growing of grain, we are not simply talking as if it was many years past of going out into fields and planting seed, hoping and praying for some sunshine and some rain so that the grain would grow and then harvesting the grain and shipping it to ports. The system today is so complex, so highly technical, it is a process that defies the imagination from the planting of the seed to its eventual use somewhere in another country in this world. Some of it will stay in Canada, but most of it will be exported to other countries, Third World countries, to feed people in China, to feed people in the Ukraine, to feed people in Poland, and to feed people in Russia.
What we have is a very complex manufacturing process in growing our grain and getting it to the eventual user in our country. That complex process requires everyone contributing his part to make sure that the process continues on its way to its eventual use.
And a good part of this government's obligation is to make sure that from the time the seed is planted to the time it is harvested and to the time it is merchandised, that the farmer, the owner, the person who is responsible for the fundamental issue in this, is recompensed for his problems. Making a car is simple; you make the car, you take it out and sell it. But grain takes from the middle of April when the crop year begins to September and that process has to be financed. All we are talking about here today is that period of time where we have the grain starting to grow to the time of its eventual processing and distribution to those people I mentioned before.
It is a complex system, and farmers are automated to the best of their ability now. Prior to April they plough the fields, till the soil and plant the seed. At all times they hope that there will be just enough rain and just enough sunshine so that they can get a crop, contrary to what we experienced last year. They tend to their crops through this period of time, and there is constant work that is involved, and then it comes time for harvest.

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
The harvesting on the prairies is done with these magnificent machines that do it in such short order today. If everything is good, they get a reasonable crop. In some years, they get a magnificent crop. In other years they get a very poor crop. On the average, crops have been good.
After harvest they can store it in their own storage areas within their farm yards, or they can load it on trucks and take it down to the terminals that store it for them. Their responsibility almost ends there, but they do not get paid for it then.
They can either handle that grain on their own, or they can give it to a pool and the pool will handle it for them. This is a process that I am talking about where they need this interest, this assistance on advance payments in order to help them continue to produce what they do and to make profit.
The system gets complex. They store it in the prairie grain elevators. Now it has to be moved from the storage facilities and the grain facilities that they have in western Canada. The Wheat Board then decides where the market is going to be. They will ship it to Prince Rupert or Vancouver, or they may decide to sell the grain to their European markets and ship it to Thunder Bay. It is easy to say that they ship it to Thunder Bay, but the process in itself is complicated.
I get back to this intricate system that we need to produce our grain harvest. It goes from the elevator, to be loaded on to a special type of railway car, and it is moved either up the mountains to Prince Rupert and Vancouver or it is moved downhill to the ports at Thunder Bay. From the yard where the cars are marshalled in these areas they are brought into the terminals and the grain elevators. I can speak with some authority about Thunder Bay. If the grain is moved into those marshalling yards, the grain is then sorted, put in different elevator bins, and cleaned. Value is added at that point, and then it is stored in another elevator.
The grain has been handled now about six times. You would think at that point we would be getting toward the end of the process, but the transportation is only the beginning. From that point in Thunder Bay we have to get the grain to a down river port.
Now comes the water transportation system in our country, the St. Lawrence Seaway. The ships are owned
by a variety of companies in this country, mostly Canadian: CSL and Patterson. They come in and load so many tonnes from the elevators on to these ships which go to Sault Ste. Marie, Toronto, through the Welland Canal, and on to what we call the down river ports in Quebec which take on this grain.
The grain is taken off the ships, put into another elevator, stored again, waiting for the offshore purchasers to take it back to their countries. So the grain, again, is sitting there and must be shipped once more on large ships which come here from Europe.
I can see my time is drawing to a close. It is important that we realize the intricacies of the growing and transporting of grain in this country, and that during the whole process, which takes several months from the time it is grown to the time it is completed, the farmer is waiting to be paid.
All this bill is trying to do is take away the money he would normally receive, this $27 million, which could finance the grain in this country waiting for shipment or sale to other parts of the country. I suggest to you this government should withdraw this bill and give the agricultural producers, the farmers of this country, an opportunity and a chance.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak for a few minutes on this bill. It is an important bill as far as many parts of the country are concerned. We have had a tendency to speak about western Canadian grain generally.
I want to point out that it has a much, much greater impact across the country than that. In the last little while in Prince Edward Island, the grain growers, vegetable growers, marketing boards, and tobacco growers were users of these particular advance payments.
In Ontario there were nine organizations that used this type of advance payment: Blue Water Storage, Cedar Springs Cherry Growers, the Ontario Soybean Growers, the Ontario Flue-cured Tobacco Growers, the Ontario Corn Producers Association, the Ontario Potato Growers Marketing Board, Timiskaming Grain Growers, Georgian Triangle Apples Limited, and the St. Lawrence Valley Fruit Growers Association. These were groups of producers which used this particular advance payment structure.
October 26, 1989

The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the Saskatchewan Beekeepers Association and the Saskatchewan Vegetable Growers also used advance payments; in Manitoba, the Honey Marketing Board and the Canola Growers; in British Columbia, the B.C. Tree Fruits Limited, B.C. Coast Vegetables, the Okanagan Fruit Producers and Shippers Association, the Island Vegetable Co-op Association, and the Interior Vegetable Agency; in Alberta, the Alberta Fresh Vegetable Marketing Board, the Potato Commission, the Alberta Honey Producers, the Wheat Pool, and the seed producers. These are some of the organizations which made use of this particular bill.
There is also the bill which deals with wheat board grains, now only barley and wheat. In the past it was barley, wheat and oats.
It is not a limited group that we are talking about here. It is farmers right across the country. What we are seeing here to some extent is the final stage of the abandoning of our old friend from Prince Albert, John Diefenbaker. As a member who represented the same constituency as Mr. Diefenbaker, I recognize the contribution that he made to agriculture and to Canada.
I recognize also, sometimes to my chagrin, the contribution that he made to the Conservative Party in this country. For years he kept that party going in the west. When they found themselves in the wilderness he was always there. Besides that, he made a contribution to this Parliament. He was one of the strongest opponents of closure. In fact, he won his first national election as Prime Minister using closure of the TransCanada PipeLines bill as the basis for his cross country campaign.
What we are seeing here is the Conservative party abandoning John Diefenbaker, what he stood for, what this Parliament stood for when he was in it, and what he stood for as far as the Conservative party was concerned. He kept the party alive and he had a real concern for farmers. In 1957 he was the person who brought into this House the Advance Payments for Prairie Grains Act. Now we have the Conservative party denying in every phase of its operations the important contribution that John Diefenbaker made to this House, to Canada, and in this particular bill to the farmers of Canada.
Government Orders
In 1977 the second bill was put into place because it was recognized that there was a need for it. The two bills have somewhat the same reason for being, but slightly different.
The Western Prairie Grains Advance Payments Act was for the marketing of wheat, barley and oats. It was put in place because there were problems with delivery. There were quota problems. You might have the grain in your bin, but there was no room in the elevator; there were no boxcars available to take it to market. It gave the prairie farmer the opportunity to keep that grain but still get enough money to pay his bills.
Therefore, it helped the farmer because he did not have to pay interest on the bills that he owed to the fertilizer supplier and the gas supplier in the community. But it helped those communities, too, because they were dependent upon farmers, for money from farmers. It got that money to those communities when they needed it.
One would think that this government is almost deliberately moving to eliminate what is rural Canada. For instance, the last speaker mentioned post offices and the elimination of transportation. If you look back at the introduction of this particular bill by the Minister of Agriculture and look at what he said, not even very indirectly, it suggests that the time has come to abandon the farmers, that they have to look at competing in a situation where they are finding themselves less and less able to compete.
What this government is going to do is pull the plug and say: "You're on your own. You pay for your insurance. If you can't pay for it, it's too bad." That kind of approach is harming the confidence of the farmers in the west and all across Canada. How much money is really involved? It is $27 million. Your friend, Mr. Speaker, Peter Pocklington, took more out of Alberta in one loan than that total amount.
Yesterday, the Auditor General tabled in this House a report that suggested there was one little loophole in the collecting of the federal sales tax that costs this government $350 million a year. This $27 million is 7.5 per cent of that loss which the government allows to slip away without any effort to collect. We are not talking about a huge amount of money. As I suggested earlier, we have two bills being amended here: The Prairie Grain Ad-

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
vance Payments Act and the Advance Payments for Crops Act.
The Advance Payments Act is for those crops which are sold on the open market. There is no pooling attempt. The price is what the farmer or the producer or the retailer can get when he sells it. The tendency for prices to go down when there is a lot of them on the market is recognized by everyone. If you dump all of the crops on to the market at the beginning of the year because farmers are short of money and need that money, the prices go down.
I grew up on the prairies when there was no Canadian Wheat Board. My father used to do his best to hang on to his wheat or his grain in the fall because it might be 75 cents or $1 a bushel in the fall, but if he could hold it until spring it would be $2 a bushel and twice as much could be made on it. The Wheat Board eliminated that for the grain growers on the prairies, but we still have a lot of farmers growing products under that basis. The Advance Payments Act allowed the evening out of that, because if all the com from Ontario arrives on the market at the same time in the fall, the price would go down and that is what the farmer would get.
If farmers receive some advance payment, the price of the corn stays up because there is not too much of it out there. As it goes on to the market gradually over the season it keeps its price. Those people buying corn know that if the price is too low they are not going to get any corn because the advance payment is there to provide the farmer with the cash when he needs it.
Com Growers of Ontario tells us that none of them or very few of them-only those who need the money for other reasons-will actually use the advance payments process if they have to pay interest on it. If you are betting that the price of corn will go up and have to pay 12 or 15 per cent interest on the money that you borrow, you are betting that the price will go up more than the 15 per cent that you will have to pay on that corn. Very few farmers are willing to take that chance.
In order to pay their bills and to assist their communities in surviving, they are going to put their grain on the market as quickly as they can, force the price down and take what they can get, with the net result that in the long ran they will be making less money. As my colleague, the member for Mackenzie pointed out, it is quite possible that the government will have to support
them under the other programs which the government has in place.
We have been told by the member for Athabasca that this bill is not being passed because of the New Democrats and the Liberals. He should recognize, as I think most of the people of the country do, that there is a bill in place. The legislation is in place. If there is the political will, as he suggests there is, all the government has to do is use the legislation and it can have that money to the farmers next week. There are some farmers who need it. There are not many who want it under the circumstances which are being suggested by the government. There are very few who need the $250,000.
The statistics show that very few of the farmers took the maximum that was available to them under the present act. The present act allowed them $30,000 if they were single farmers, $60,000 if there were two people involved, and $90,000 as a maximum in a corporation or a triple partnership.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Now they will get $250,000 if they need it.
So if they need $250,000 and they have to pay interest on it why would they do it, particularly if they are doing it because the prices-
Because they are getting it cheaper than they can get it anywhere else.

That is exactly the reason. The member for Athabasca is reinforcing my argument. If you have to pay interest on it and you are taking that loan out because you are waiting for the price to go up, you are betting. You pay 15 per cent for that loan and the price only goes up 10 per cent, what have you gained?
Nothing.

Nothing at all. My friend from Athabasca suggested that this bill was here in June. It was here in June. It was so bad that nobody wanted it. The government brought it in on June 25, the last day that we sat in this House and wanted it all passed in one day.
Those of us who saw the bill thought that it was so ridiculous that we laughed. The government saw it was ridiculous too and removed it. The bill came back in the

fall only slightly changed. It came back the second time in September as a different bill.

The bill was brought before us in September, but it was so bad and had so many flaws in it that the government withdrew it. That was Bill C-32. It withdrew that in the House on October 3.
A few days ago, we reached the eighth hour of debate. This bill upon which the government has brought closure has had maybe eight hours and 10 minutes of debate. The government says that is enough debate. We have had a little more than two days of debate, and it is quite out of line with the tradition of this House to bring in closure at that point. It implies the government is afraid that if the farmers know too much about the bill that they will not accept it and the government might lose some of the support of the farmers.
Traditionally the Conservatives have had a lot of support in the rural areas, but they are losing it because they are bringing in ill conceived and underdeveloped legislation such as this.
The reason the government gave us for bringing this bill in and putting interest on the advances to farmers had nothing to do with the value to the farmers, it was more to do with deficit reduction.
Who caused the inflation in this country that led to this problem? It certainly was not the farmers. The farmers got a billion dollars of help in the last couple of years. Some will say that they are getting too much. But that has been returned to the country many times over by the farmers, even in these last two years, because the total production of the farm community has been increasing, even as they have been making less money. What is a fair share for the farmers to pay? What we are asking the farmers to do is add to a debt that they already have.
Government Orders
The farmers are already in trouble with debt. The last thing farmers need is more debt. This is what the farmers are being asked to do in this particular case. They are being asked to take an advance, an interest bearing debt, to increase the debt. The irony is that the farmers who are going to possibly borrow the $250,000 are the ones who are so deperately badly off now that nobody will give them money in any other way. That is the only reason why the $250,000 is there, Mr. Speaker.
As I said before, every group of farmers across the country has used, in some way, this advance payment structure. We should be doing what we can to keep that kind of structure in place so that the farmers can make the market work better and work for them. If you force them to take less for their product, many more farmers will have to leave the industry. We should be trying to keep them there, not eliminating them. We have no intention of supporting this bill under its present structure.

Mr. Speaker, I too appreciate the opportunity to address this bill. We have heard today how this amending legislation does not change the spirit and intent of the two acts, and I want to add to that.
First, as before, the Advance Payments for Crops Act will help producers store crops after harvest and spread deliveries over the entire marketing season to take advantage of stronger prices.
Second, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act will ease pressure on the quota delivery system and reduce congestion at local elevators.
Third, the loan guarantee components of these acts are to remain intact.
The federal government will continue to guarantee the principal amount advanced to the farmers under the various programs. While we are amending the advance payments act in order to remove the interest-free provisions, it has also provided us with an opportunity to enhance these acts.
As I understand it, consultations were held with the producers and their organizations throughout the summer. These consultations have now resulted in improvements contained in the bill before this House.

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
In order to make advances available under both acts, as soon as possible after this bill is given Royal Assent, regulations will no longer be used to establish maximum interest rates covered under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. In the future the maximum interest rates to be guaranteed under the program will be determined by the Minister of Agriculture, prime or less than prime.
Under the current Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, regulation sets the maximum rate of interest which the government will guarantee in the event a producer defaults on a loan. No such amendment is required to the Advance Payments for Crops Act since such provisions were added to the legislation in 1985. To ensure that advance payments under both acts are available as soon as possible after Bill C-36 has received Royal Assent, it is proposed that the minister also set the interest rates which are to be covered by the Canadian Wheat Board.
If we continue to rely on regulations, this would mean an undue delay on advance payments to western wheat and barley producers, many of whom are in my constituency of Wetaskiwin. These producers would be forced to wait for new regulations before they could take advantage of the program.
Since a similar change to the Advance Payments for Crops Act has proven successful, we should proceed as quickly as possible with this amendment to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. Producers participating in this program, especially those of my constituency, should not face delays in receiving their advances. By removing the need for regulations, the government is ensuring that those western grain producers who have come to rely on advance payment programs can do so again and as soon as possible. I believe this can only be an enhanced benefit for my area.

The hon. member for Burlington should be ashamed to be supporting a government that is so arrogant and so willing to trample on the rights of Parliament.
Here is what the hon. member for Vegreville had to say on that occasion in 1983. He stated: "I really regret
what the minister has done today". I assume these were not crocodile tears. He continues:
The position of this party has been one of constructive criticism,
months and months of it, but that did not matter:
We have offered alternatives, tried to improve the Bill and seek out reasonable solutions. But the minister is so skittish about his own bill that he has to move closure. He will not allow the alternatives to be debated.
Nine days of debate at second reading, three months in committee with over 200 witnesses, 15 days in the report stage in the House and here is the Deputy Prime Minister saying the minister would not allow the alternatives to be debated. What would he say today if he were here discussing this bill in this debate. He would say we have not had an opportunity to discuss this thing. He would say our rights are being trampled on, if he followed his example. But oh, no, there is more. On page 28353 of Hansard he states:
Here we have an opportunity to debate some of the positive alternatives advanced by our Party, and that is being denied.
What about us? What about the denial of our rights as members of Parliament to discuss this bill after 4 days, not 24, which is what the hon. member for Vegreville had in 1983. He continues:
Rather than working toward a solution, the Government decided to use force.
What is the government doing here? Raw force, Mr. Speaker, for the eighth time in this Parliament. He goes on:
Members opposite suggest they are acting in the best interest of the country because they are being stubborn.
That is the kind of language he was using. On the same page. He states:
-we in our Party have tried to work toward a positive and satisfactory solution. We have opposed and we have proposed. We have offered alternatives. We have listened to the evidence before the committee- But we are very saddened by the fact-
It almost makes one weep, Mr. Speaker.
-that we have not been able to debate the alternative proposals we believe would go a long way toward improving this Bill.
To debate the alternative proposals, my foot. He had 24 days to debate the alternative proposals; 97 members spoke on second reading alone, and here is the Deputy Prime Minister shedding these crocodile tears, spouting this stuff and nonsense about not having an opportunity to debate. Why is he not up here saying we have not had a fair opportunity today if he believed that then? We have had only four days at second reading on this bill and
October 26, 1989

one of them was a half day. We have had nine hours of debate on this bill and here closure is being moved again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: That is all it needs.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I say it is an absolute disgrace.
I have more because we have the Minister of Justice to deal with now. I am sure if he is watching this on television he must be getting very nervous because in a debate in 1984 on a time allocation motion on a Borrowing Authority Bill, the Minister of Justice decided to get into the act and he made a remark about closure. It is a very short remark but I think it is very instructive. At page 2518 of Hansard March 28, 1984 he stated:
But closure is the problem of the Liberal Party.
That is what the Minister of Justice said. The man who has introduced closure more than any other House Leader ever in Canada had the nerve to say in 1984 that closure was the problem of the Liberal Party.
If it was the problem of the Liberal Party, it is the problem of the Tory party today because they have shamefully abused the trust that was placed in them by the Canadian people last November by applying closure at every stage of every bill in this House. It is an indictment I would be ashamed of were I sitting on the other side of the House.
Let us look at the record on that bill when the Minister of Justice had the unmitigated gall to make that statement. Bill C-21 had been debated-let us listen to the dates, the hon. member for Burlington might find this interesting-on March 7, March 8, March 13, March 14, March 15, March 20, March 21, March 27, March 28. Those are the dates it was debated on second reading. It was at that point they brought in this time allocation order to get the bill through.
Have we had debate of that magnitude on this bill? No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You have had plenty of debate. Why don't you want to help the farmers of the country.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
No. Have we had it on any of the bills on which closure has been moved in this House? No. We have not. Closure has been rammed down our throats at
Government Orders
every turn by this government and it is a shocking indictment.
Here is another quote by the Minister of Justice, as he now is. He said on page 2519 of XHansardo of the same date:
"It is very unfortunate that the Liberal Party is cutting off debate on this Bill and, naturally, our Party will be voting against the motion to cut debate.
Here we have this absolute two-faced nonsense from this minister who, after all those days of debate, eight days of debate, now says that after four days we have had too much. Three and a half, as a matter of fact. It is quite unsatisfactory.
Let me turn to the bill. This bill, as the honourable member for Halifax says, is pernicious. When the government could be paying this money out to the farmers today, it is sitting back waiting for this bill to pass and saying the reason the farmers do not have it is because of us. It has worked itself into a comer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are against the farmers.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Niagara Falls is here and he seems to think the farmers are not with us. Again, if I was the Deputy Prime Minister, I would be quaking in my boots with the letters we are getting on these things.
Let me read this letter into the record. It comes from the President of the Manitoba Canola Growers Association. The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds is very fond of telling us how he has these people in his pocket, that they support this legislation, that they think it is the greatest thing since sliced bread. Let us hear what they think about this.
Let me read this letter dated October 20 from the President of the Manitoba Granola Growers Association and see what they think about this legislation. The letter is addressed to my colleague, the agriculture critic, the hon. member for Algoma. It states:
We would like to encourage your continued support for reinstatement of the interest-free provision for the cash advance programs. Without the reinstatement of said provision, the program holds little benefit for Canadian farmers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sure my hon. friend would like to keep the record

Government Orders
straight. Granola you buy in grocery stores, granola bars and so on. I think he is referring to canola growers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: He has no idea.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize. Of course I meant canola. I thank the hon. member for Athabasca for his very helpful intervention. I am delighted to receive help from the other side. Let me continue reading the letter:
With respect to oilseeds, the interest-free cash advance has contributed to orderly delivery, by removing the pressure on producers to sell at harvest, a time when prices tend to trend down.
Further, one of our Board members happens to be the person responsible for administering the Canola Cash Advance Program offered under the Prairie Canola Growers Council. His calculations show that with the fee which must be charged to cover the costs of administering the program the true cost of the advance would be prime plus at least one or two percent. Because the administration fee is a fixed amount no matter the size of the loan, the shorter the period for which the loan is held and the smaller the amount borrowed, the higher the actual interest rate becomes, making it more economical for farmers under those circumstances to borrow directly from a lending institution. As a result, the cash advance loses all usefulness.
In other words, this man is saying this bill is absolutely useless for these growers.
I will continue reading the letter:
While our organization's interest is solely canola, none of our members grow only canola. Consequently, I feel it reasonable to also make a comment on the advance program for grains marketed by the Canadian Wheat Board. I think it only fair, that as long as Canadian farmers must operate under a system which requires them to hold grain in on-farm storage, that we should be reimbursed for that storage. The cash advance program as it has been in the past at least provided some consideration in that direction.
Would you please let our office know when Bill C-36 goes to committee as we are interested in submitting a brief.
They are opposed to this bill, they have sense. The letter is signed by Mr. Max Polon, President of the Manitoba Canola Growers Association. These people realize what a disaster this bill is for the farming community in Canada.
I have more. An article appeared in The Kingston Whig-Standard just today. One of my constituents, who happens to be the president of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, Mrs. Brigid Pyke, had this to say, according to the article:
Farmers will soon learn whether the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement has killed the small family farm in Canada, says Brigid Pyke, President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. Mrs. Pyke says that weak bargaining by Canada during the free trade negotiations allowed the U.S. control of farm products coming into its country, but no such power for Canada.
I could go on to read the rest of the article, but the message is clear. This government and its supporters who are bellowing away from their seats clearly have it in their minds that they are doing the farmers a favour by this bill, but every farm organization in Canada says this is not the kind of favour they need. With friends like them, they say to us, who needs enemies.
This is taking money away from farmers. Government members admit it. They stand up and say, "We are awfully sorry to be taking this money away,"-and they shed crocodile tears at the prospect-but they say, "We have to do it to balance the budget." Having run up the national debt to double what it was when the Conservatives took office, they now feel that it has become an urgent priority. I can understand why they think so. If I had botched the economy as badly as the Minister of Finance has botched it I would be running around talking about the deficit all the time too, and that is what he does. He has managed to work the hon. member for Burlington into a lather about it, obviously, because he sits there and makes comments from his seat. I invite him to participate in this debate. I do not think he has made a speech on this bill yet. I would be glad to hear from him.
As I said at the outset, and I will terminate my comments in a very short time, I have to say how sorry I am to have to participate in this debate because not being a farmer and not knowing a great deal about farming, I will admit to some ignorance on that subject. But I know when people are being taken, I know when people are being had, and that is what is being done by this government, by this bill, and I am not going to sit idly by when closure is invoked and stay silent while the farmers get shafted by this government.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak this evening on this particular debate, and I am sure that my colleagues across are all looking forward to my contribution, as you are Mr. Speaker.
October 26, 1989

I see, of course, that some Conservative members perhaps thought, mistakenly of course, that this debate would finish early, that they could go home early tonight and that the Opposition would allow the government to run roughshod over the rights of Canadian farmers. Well, not so, not so. We in the Opposition stand up for the Canadian farmers. We want to help them, and we are against the government across the way and what it is trying to do.
I have here a newsletter of the Ontario Corn Producers' Association, an organization from my province of Ontario. There are a large number of com producers, as most hon. members will know, in the great riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, as there are in the riding of Stormont-Dundas, so ably represented by my colleague sitting near me here.
I want to read what the com producers were saying in the September newsletter. They spoke first of the Ontario Minister of Agriculture. Ontario got a brand new Minister of Agriculture, a Liberal Minister of Agriculture, and here is what was said about this Liberal Minister of Agriculture:
OCPA welcomes David Ramsay to the position of Minister of Agriculture and Food in Ontario. Mr. Ramsay won a lot of friends with his openness and honesty in answering questions following his luncheon speech at our semi-annual convention on September 6 at the Waterloo Inn -
We also express our thanks to Jack Riddell for his 4-year span as ag. minister in the province. While Jack was well-known for his "devil's advocate" approach in examining requests and advice provided by producer organizations, we always found him to be a good listener, generally receptive to well-researched proposals, and totally dedicated to the well-being of rural Ontario.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, being the non-partisan person you are, that those farmers have nothing but praise for the two Liberal ministers of agriculture in Ontario, Mr. Riddell, the predecessor, and Mr. Ramsay, the new minister. Those are the comments that these people had to make.
Let me read a little bit further where these people speak about advance payments. They say the following:
There is little to add to our comments of previous newsletters, and to the announcement that appears in this magazine, other than the statement made recently by a special assistant to the Agriculture Minister Don Mazankowski that no program will be offered until the Act is amended (to eliminate the interest-free provision) and new regulations are completed. At present, it remains OCPA policy to
Government Orders
oppose the changes (at least until such time as comparable changes are made in the U.S. Farm Bill), as we believe that any benefit conferred via an interest-bearing program will be eliminated via the myriad of administrative procedures (and costs borne by producers) which this program entails. It's an unfortunate situation because there are signs, according to some analysts, that storage after harvest could be beneficial during the coming crop marketing year.
They are talking about the two provincial Liberal ministers of agriculture, and they say what a fine job they are doing. They only mention in one paragraph the federal government and condemn the fact that the program that they announced in Bill C-36 is lousy. That is the difference. It is time that the members across the way started listening to that. This is not the Liberal policy book. This is the Ontario Corn Producers' newsletter from which I have been reading.
The member across the way is from Ontario and perhaps there is not much com grown in his constituency, but whether there is or is not, the consumers of Ontario are nevertheless, in the long ran, paying directly or indirectly. Of course, damage to the farmers of Ontario and to Canadian farmers generally is damage to the Canadian consumer because in the long run, the loss of a good agricultural economy is not just a loss to the farmers but to society as a whole.
I have here a letter that was written to the Minister of Agriculture dated June 5, 1989. Perhaps some of my colleagues referred to this earlier tonight, but it bears repeating. It states:
The Ontario Com Producers' Association and the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board are opposed to the announcement contained in the April budget that calls for the elimination of the interest free provision of the Advance Payments for Crops Act.
They are opposed to it. We are hearing from the Minister of Agriculture and from his Associate Minister through planted questions that come from the back row of the Conservative side that somehow people are in favour of this bill. Of course we are in favour of advance payments, but we are not in favour of a bill that will remove the interest-free provisions. That is what we are against. Planting questions through back-benchers will not solve this. What will solve this is a realization by the government that this measure it is trying to impose upon the House tonight using all kinds of methods to stifle debate will not work.

October 26, 1989
Government Orders
Oh, yes, sooner or later when we run out of speakers, the government will get its bill, but it will not get the support and approval of Canadians. It will not get the support and approval of farmers across Canada. Yes, a few trained seals in the back row will applaud when the Minister of Agriculture stands to vote, and the Minister of Agriculture will pretend that that is synonymous with the approval of the Canadian people, but he is wrong. He is wrong if that is what he thinks.
I say to those government members across the way that there is still time for them to go out to the lobby to shake up the Minister of Agriculture, to tell him to withdraw the bill, to start over, to do it properly, and to listen to the great recommendations made by my honourable and very distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, who at one time was also a Minister of Agriculture and a great one at that, and to listen to the recommendations of my colleague from Algoma, who similarly has a lot of experience in representing farmers as the opposition agriculture critic for many years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Do the corn producers refer to him too in their newsletter?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The member across the way asked if the corn producers, in their newsletter, referred to one opposition member versus another. The important thing is that the corn producers refer to the minister and to his policies and they say that the minister's policies are lousy. That is what is important for my colleague across the way to remember. What is so unfortunate is that the members across the way, in spite of the fact that we have repeated it over and over again, fail to understand.
I know you understand, Mr. Speaker, because you are a non-partisan person, and you understand that fully. But the members across the way are not nearly as objective as you and I. They do not understand nearly as well. Perhaps by stating and restating it, we will convince them of the fact that this bill as presently drafted is not in the best interests of Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, in my riding there are a number of corn growers, a number of farmers, as you know, and I have mentioned this many times in the House of Commons. Our farmers are sick and tired of hearing about cuts, cuts
and more cuts every time the budget comes around, cuts that always have a disastrous impact on the agricultural sector, cuts that are always imposed by a Minister of Finance who seems totally impervious to the fact that Canadian agriculture is suffering, a Minister who seems totally indifferent to the fact that our Canadian farmers will find it increasingly hard to cope as a result of so-called free trade. Mr. Speaker, all I can say is that the Minister of Finance and all his fellow members opposite better start listening to the Official Opposition and to Canadian farmers. They know what they need. They know that during the past few years, the present Government has imposed cutbacks that are entirely unreasonable, considering the problems I mentioned earlier.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to make a last appeal to hon. members opposite, and ask them once again to forget the Minister of Finance, to forget the fact that in 15 or 20 minutes they will be thanked for voting the right way. I ask them to consider something far more important, their own constituents, and above all, I ask them to consider Canada's producers and farmers this evening. It is high time we started thinking about our farmers and forgot the bankers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if there might be a predisposition to apply the previous vote to the current vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to consider the suggestion of the government Whip.
I think, if you were to ask the House for unanimous consent, we could dispense with the taking of the vote and apply the result of the previous one.

Bill read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the representative of the government House leader to tell us what the business of the House will be for tomorrow and hopefully beyond that.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government House leader anticipated being here for a 1 a.m. vote and bringing the information on the business of the House with him on that occasion.
The surprise ending of the debate and the quickness of the vote make it clear that he is not here with us and that that information is with him. We will share it will all members of the House as quickly as possible upon his arrival. The House will start at ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I appreciate the difficult position the government Whip finds himself in, I do not think it says much for the government's respect for Parliament not to be able at this time to say what business the government intends to call.
I would suggest that if government members would like to stay here until one o'clock, we could easily arrange it. I hope the government will realize that it is not only showing disrespect for this House but for the parliamentary process not to be able to say what the business is. I hope the Canadian people will realize how incapable the government is of managing the business of the House.
